The scored earth told him something had changed.

Luca crouched at the edge of the grove, fourteen years old and certain of very little except what the ground beneath his feet could show him. Three days ago, after the storm that had broken across the Pollino peaks with the force of divine anger, he'd come here as he came most days—to move the sheep, to check the water source, to sit in the shade of the old Bosnian pine that rose like a weathered sentinel above the limestone scattered across the hillside. The tree had always been here, longer than the village had kept its records. Longer, he suspected, than anyone living could remember.

But three days ago, something about it had shifted.

The roots, which he'd memorized over countless visits the way another boy might memorize the names of saints, no longer lay in their familiar pattern. The northern anchor, the one that had always pressed deepest into the scored stone, had moved. Not much. Perhaps a hand's breadth. But it had moved, and the earth around it bore the evidence—raw limestone scratched pale where the roots had torn free, a subtle depression where they had previously settled, and that scored earth, that fresh destruction of the orderly arrangement he had always seen.

He'd said nothing to anyone. Not yet.

The tree itself rose before him now, its dark needles absorbing the thin autumn light. The trunk was ancient, gnarled with centuries of weather, its bark thick and furrowed enough that a man could hide his fingers in the cracks. The resin had wept from several places on the south face, dark and glossy now that it had dried, crusted like old blood.

Luca placed his palm against the bark.

It was warm. Not from the sunlight—the afternoon was cooling, and the sun sat low enough that the grove was mostly shadow. The warmth came from within, steady and deliberate, pulsing very faintly beneath his hand like a heartbeat that had nothing to do with flesh or blood.

He jerked his hand away.

The tree was a tree. Trees did not move. Trees did not have heartbeats. Trees did not leave scored earth and torn roots and evidence of displacement that a shepherd boy could read like scripture written in stone and soil.

He stood, suddenly aware that his legs had begun to shake. The slopes around him were empty—the sheep were grazing two hundred paces down the hill, and no one else came to this part of the Pollino except the monks from the lower monastery when they needed medicinal herbs. Still, he felt watched. The feeling was not new to the mountains; a man who lived among rock and wind learned early to sense the attentiveness of the landscape. But this felt different. This felt like being observed by something that was aware of his observation.

Luca turned and walked back down to the sheep. His usual practice was to spend most of his time in the grove, reading the weather in the wind and the ground, letting the animals drift where they would. Today, he drove them farther down the slope, toward the lower pasture where the grass was thinner but where, at least, he could not see the old tree against the sky.

He returned the next morning.

The displacement had grown. The root system, which had always seemed almost deliberately anchored to catch water from multiple sources, had rearranged itself further. The northern anchor had moved again, just slightly, but definitely. And the soil where the roots had been was disturbed—not dramatically, not in a way that would be obvious to a casual observer, but the pattern was wrong. The displacement was coherent. It was directional.

It was as though the tree was moving deliberately northward.

Luca told himself this was impossible. He was a shepherd, not a scholar. He knew animals and weather and the behavior of plants well enough to predict the seasons and read the health of grazing land, but he understood that knowledge was a small thing, contained within the narrow bounds of practical necessity. Whatever was happening here fell outside those bounds entirely.

He came back the next day. And the next. Each time, the evidence accumulated. The roots had progressed further north, and the soil bore the marks of deliberate repositioning. The tree's lean had changed minutely, as though its center of gravity was slowly shifting. The resin weeping from the south face had increased—he could see the trail of it now, dark and thick, running down the bark like a scar.

His father noticed his absences first.

"You're spending too much time in the high pasture," his father said on the fifth day, when Luca returned to the village near dusk, having spent nearly the entire day in the grove. "The sheep don't need that much watching. They need watching, but not that much."

"The grass is better up there," Luca said, which was true. It was also only a partial truth.

"The grass was fine last month," his father replied. His father was a practical man, concerned with practicalities—the movement of animals, the management of land, the simple transactions that kept a shepherd's life moving forward. He had no patience for nuance. "Your mother is beginning to think you're not interested in the village anymore."

Luca had no response to that. His mother had always been more perceptive than his father, and if she was already noticing his pattern, it would not be long before more people began to wonder why a shepherd boy was spending so much time alone in the high Pollino, away from the established routes and the common grazing areas.

Still, he went back.

By the eighth day, the tree's movement had become undeniable. The trunk itself had shifted position, leaning more distinctly toward the north and slightly west. The roots had spread in that direction, seeking something—new soil, new water sources, new mineral composition in the limestone. The resin weeping had become profuse, dark streams running down the bark, pooling at the base where the roots met the earth. When Luca touched it, it was hot, almost uncomfortably so, and it left a sticky residue on his fingers that smelled of something acrid and resinous, unfamiliar.

It was during his observation of this resin—crouching at the base of the tree, carefully examining the fluid and trying to determine what might cause such profuse weeping—that he first became aware of being watched.

The awareness arrived without warning. Luca was entirely focused on the resin, on running his fingers along the texture of the pooled liquid, on trying to parse some meaning from the tree's visible distress. And then, as suddenly as thought arriving unbidden, he understood that someone was looking at him.

He straightened so quickly that his vision momentarily blurred. The slopes around the grove were empty. He could see the entire approach from above, the paths that descended from the higher peaks toward the monastery lands, the broader route that led toward the village. All empty. Only the wind moved across the stone, carrying the particular scent of high autumn, cold and dry and faintly resinous.

But the sensation did not fade. Someone was watching him from concealment, with the kind of patient attention that suggested long, steady observation.

Luca gathered himself deliberately. He was fourteen, which meant he was old enough to manage sheep and young enough to be entirely conscious of his vulnerability in the mountains. There were stories about the high Pollino, stories that circulated in the village in the evening, about men who had ventured into the peaks and never returned, about bandits and monks and other creatures whose names were never spoken plainly.

He walked back toward the village slowly, trying not to appear alarmed. Behind him, the old tree stood in its altered position, still weeping resin, still impossibly moved from where it had always been.

He did not return for two days. His father had noticed his absences too directly, and his mother had begun asking pointed questions about his time in the hills. Instead, Luca worked the lower pastures, herding sheep through the thinning grass, trying not to think about roots and resin and the sensation of being observed by something he could not see.

On the third day, the pressure of not knowing became unbearable. He rose before dawn, told his parents he was taking the sheep to the northern grazing area, and climbed back toward the grove.

The tree had moved again. This time, the displacement was so significant that he could not dismiss it as the work of weather or imagination. The trunk leaned noticeably farther to the north. The root system had spread in that direction with clear intention, and fresh earth was disturbed in a pattern that suggested methodical relocation. The resin had stopped weeping quite so profusely, but it had hardened in dark, glossy trails down the bark, marking the path of the weeping like a record of pain or effort.

Luca stood before the tree for a long time, trying to reconcile what he was seeing with what he understood to be possible. The tree was moving. It was moving deliberately, methodically, in a northward direction. It was moving, and this movement was impossible, which meant either that he was experiencing some form of profound delusion, or that the world contained mysteries that extended far beyond the reasonable boundaries of a shepherd boy's understanding.

He was still standing there, hand raised to the bark, when the voice spoke behind him.

"You've noticed."

Luca spun so quickly that he nearly fell. The man standing at the edge of the grove was perhaps fifty years old, though the light was uncertain and his weathered face made his actual age difficult to determine. He was dressed in the rough wool of a mountain monk, and his dark hair was streaked with gray. But it was his hands that caught Luca's attention—they bore old scarring, glossy and pale against his weathered skin, the kind of scarring that suggested electrical injury or severe burning.

"I've been watching you watch it," the man continued. His voice was low and practical, neither kind nor unkind, simply stating fact. "For eight days now. You come, you look, you touch the bark, you try to understand what you're seeing. You do it quietly, which is good. Quietly is important."

Luca's mouth was dry. "What is it?" he asked. "What is the tree?"

The man was silent for a long moment. He looked past Luca at the old pine, examining it with the kind of attention that suggested he had seen it many times before, in many different conditions.

"What does your father do?" the man asked finally.

"He's a shepherd," Luca said.

"And before that, his father?"

"Also a shepherd," Luca said. "My family has been here for... a long time."

"Yes," the man said. "You're rooted here. You understand land and animals and how the seasons work. You're beginning to understand that some things don't fit into those patterns. That's the question you're asking yourself now, isn't it? How something like that—" he gestured toward the tree with one scarred hand, "—can exist when it contradicts everything you know."

"Can you explain it?" Luca asked. He heard his own voice shake slightly.

"No," the man said simply. "Not in a way that would matter. But I can tell you this: it's not the kind of thing you ask questions about in the village. It's not the kind of thing you mention to your family, or to the monks, or to anyone else. It's the kind of thing you keep to yourself, and you learn to see without drawing attention to what you're seeing."

"Why?" Luca asked.

"Because people fear what they don't understand," the man said. "And fear makes them dangerous. If people understood what that tree is, what it can do, what it means—they would try to destroy it, or control it, or study it until it died from too much attention. The only thing that keeps it safe is silence. The only thing that keeps you safe, if you intend to stay near it, is learning to be silent too."

Luca swallowed. "Why are you telling me this? If silence is so important, why are you speaking to me now?"

"Because you've already seen it," the man said. "And you'll keep coming back. Your curiosity is the kind that won't be satisfied by leaving it alone. I can tell. I was like that once." He paused, and for just a moment, his expression shifted to something that might have been sadness or memory or both. "I could pretend I haven't seen you, let you figure out your own way to conceal what you know, hope you don't draw attention to yourself through clumsiness. Or I can tell you the only thing that matters: if you intend to come here, if you intend to keep watching and learning, you need a reason that will convince your family, a reason that makes sense."

"What reason?" Luca asked.

"Prayer," the man said. "Tell them you've taken to praying in the high places. That it's brought you closer to God, or that you believe God speaks more clearly in the mountains than in the village. Most monks are sympathetic to that kind of thing. Your family might be too, eventually. And prayer is something you can do alone, something that requires no witnesses, something that explains long absences without requiring explanation. You can pray for hours and no one will question why."

The man turned to leave, then paused. "My name is Farovald," he said. "If you see me again, be careful not to acknowledge me. We don't know each other. We've never spoken."

"Wait—" Luca said, but the man was already moving back down the slope, his movement surprisingly efficient for someone his apparent age. Within moments, he had disappeared into the rocks and scrub vegetation, and Luca was alone in the grove again with the tree and the weight of what he had just learned.

He stood there for a long time, hand on the warm bark, feeling the steady pulse of something moving beneath the skin of wood and resin. Then he turned and walked back down the mountain.

## The Storm Before

Two hundred years earlier, in the year 589 of the Christian calendar, the Pollino Mountains held a secret that neither the Lombards nor the few remaining Byzantine settlers could have imagined.

The lightning had come with a storm that bent the peaks like grass in wind. Rain fell in sheets thick enough to blind, and the lightning tracked from cloud to earth with a frequency that made the entire landscape flicker between visibility and darkness, between the world as it appeared in daylight and the world stripped down to bone and shadow.

The old Bosnian pine had stood in that place for centuries, its roots deep in the mineral-rich limestone, its connection to the soil absolute and unchanging. It was the kind of tree that a man might pass a dozen times in a life and never truly see—old enough to be invisible, established enough to seem permanent, the sort of landmark that becomes part of the landscape rather than an object within it.

The lightning struck it directly.

The electrical force traveled through the mature wood, through the cambium where growth happened cell by cell, through the root system that reached into the limestone and the specialized fungal network that had evolved alongside it for millennia. The strike left scars—darkened wood, burned bark, resin weeping from wounds that would never fully heal. The force of the electricity restructured the cellular tissue of the root system at a microscopic level, loosening the rigid connections that bound the tree to immobility, introducing a kind of electrochemical malleability into structures that had always been designed for permanence.

And in the moment of the strike, a man who had been sheltering beneath the tree—seeking protection from the rain on a route that should have avoided the storm but had not—felt the same lightning pass through him. His hands, placed against the bark when the strike came, received the full force of the electrical burn. His body, already sensitive to the earth's electrical currents in ways that would not be understood for another thousand years, underwent a transformation that would alter the remaining centuries of his life.

The man's name was Farovald, and he was thirty-nine years old when the lightning made him something other than mortal.

He staggered away from the tree when the strike ended, his burned hands hanging useless at his sides, his body convulsing with the aftereffects of the electricity. He did not understand what had happened to him. He could not have understood it—the mechanisms were too far beyond the knowledge of his time, too deeply embedded in the biology of specialized adaptation that would only be discovered and named centuries later.

But he understood that he had been touched by something vast and terrible, that it had rewritten some essential part of him, and that whatever had happened in that moment would color the remainder of his existence in ways he could not yet begin to comprehend.

The tree, in its own way, understood much the same thing.

For two hundred years, Italus and Farovald would exist in a strange parallel existence, never truly together but fundamentally connected by the singularity of that moment. The tree would learn, very slowly, to move through the soil and stone of the Pollino. The man would learn, even more slowly, that aging had become optional, that his body would repair itself from injuries that should have been fatal, that the decades would stretch out before him in a way that no other human would ever experience.

And the secret of that moment, that shared transformation, would be kept by both of them in the only way such secrets could be kept—through silence, through concealment, through the careful management of knowledge and the deliberate construction of distance from the understanding of ordinary men.

The storm passed, as all storms do. The lightning moved on to strike other peaks, other trees, other lives that it would alter without intention or malice. The rain eased and eventually ceased. The clouds broke, and the Pollino emerged again into daylight, changed in some ways and entirely unchanged in others.

A man walked down from the mountains with burned hands and no explanation for them, and a tree began, so slowly that centuries would pass before the change became truly evident, to move.

Luca did not sleep much that night. He lay on his pallet in the corner of his family's small stone house and listened to the sounds of the village settling into darkness. His father's snoring from the inner room. The dogs moving restlessly in the yard. The sound of wind in the eaves, bringing with it the scent of autumn and stone and distant resin.

He understood, in the way that young people sometimes understand things without being taught them, that he had crossed some kind of threshold. That the world he inhabited before this moment—the simple world of seasons and animals and the repetitive work that filled a shepherd's days—was no longer entirely real to him. He had seen something that should not exist, and he had been told by a stranger with burned hands and old eyes that the only appropriate response was silence.

Silence and prayer.

The next morning, before his family rose, Luca went to his mother.

"I've been thinking about taking up prayer," he told her. "More seriously. The monks say God speaks more clearly in the high places."

His mother looked at him with an expression that contained both surprise and something like satisfaction. She was a woman of faith, or at least of the practical faith that one maintained in a small village where the alternative to faith was to confront the randomness and violence of existence directly.

"That's good," she said. "The monks will help you. You can go to the monastery, ask for guidance. They like young people who are serious about their faith."

His father, when told, simply grunted acknowledgment. Prayer was not something he was interested in, but it was not something he would forbid either. If his son wanted to spend time with monks and in contemplative practice, it was a respectable use of a young man's time.

And so Luca began his first practice of concealment.

He would rise early, tell his family he was going to the high pastures, and walk instead toward the monastery. Sometimes he did actually visit the monks, listening to their teachings about the nature of God and the soul and the proper way to conduct a Christian life. Mostly, though, he would turn off the main path before reaching the monastery and climb higher into the Pollino, toward the grove and the tree that was, impossibly, learning to move.

He studied the displacement patterns with the focus of a scholar, though he was no scholar. He noted the direction of movement, the speed at which the roots progressed, the way the trunk's lean shifted with the seasons. He began to understand, through close observation, something of the mechanism by which the tree accomplished its slow relocation—the way the roots that served as anchors would tighten, creating tension, then release, and the trunk would settle slightly into a new position. The resin would bleed, the roots would rest, and then the process would begin again.

He never saw Farovald again during those early years, though he became aware of being watched occasionally, a presence in the mountains that observed his observation but never made itself known. The man had given him one piece of advice, and Luca had made it his philosophy: he kept silent. He asked no questions in the village about moving trees or strange men with burned hands. He did not discuss what he saw, even with himself, except in the form of the careful records he began to keep, hidden in a small leather journal that he carried in his pack.

These records were written in a kind of shorthand, using symbols and abbreviated phrases that would mean nothing to anyone who happened to discover them. He recorded the position of the roots, the angle of the trunk's lean, the presence or absence of resin weeping. He recorded the dates, the weather, the patterns he observed. He was constructing a record of something that should not be recordable, something that existed outside the ordinary boundaries of natural law.

He was, without knowing it, beginning the practice that would define his entire life. He was becoming a guardian, taking on the responsibility of witnessing and maintaining the secret of a tree that moved and a transformation that could not be explained.

The years passed.

Luca grew older. His voice deepened. His shoulders broadened from the work of herding and climbing. His knowledge of the mountains expanded from the areas around the village to more distant peaks, more remote valleys. And all the while, the tree continued its slow progression northward, and Luca continued to watch, to record, to maintain his silence.

He never spoke of it to anyone. Not his parents, not the monks, not the other shepherd boys who occasionally ventured into the high pastures. The secret became so much a part of him that he sometimes forgot it was a secret at all. It simply became his life—a hidden life alongside the visible one, a current running beneath the surface of his days that no one else could perceive.

Until the day, many years later, when he would discover that others had been keeping the same silence, had been guarding the same secret, and that the responsibility he had assumed alone would, eventually, need to be shared.

But that was still in the future. For now, in the cool darkness of autumn, with the Pollino settling into winter and the evidence of the tree's movement hidden beneath snow that would erase the scored earth, Luca lay awake and understood that he had been chosen for something, though he did not yet understand what, or why, or for how long the burden would rest upon his shoulders.

Two hundred years earlier, in the year 589 of the Christian calendar, the Pollino Mountains held a secret that neither the Lombards nor the few remaining Byzantine settlers could have imagined.

The lightning had come with a storm that bent the peaks like grass in wind. Rain fell in sheets thick enough to blind, and the lightning tracked from cloud to earth with a frequency that made the entire landscape flicker between visibility and darkness, between the world as it appeared in daylight and the world stripped down to bone and shadow.

The old Bosnian pine had stood in that place for centuries, its roots deep in the mineral-rich limestone, its connection to the soil absolute and unchanging. It was the kind of tree that a man might pass a dozen times in a life and never truly see—old enough to be invisible, established enough to seem permanent, the sort of landmark that becomes part of the landscape rather than an object within it.

The lightning struck it directly.

The electrical force traveled through the mature wood, through the cambium where growth happened cell by cell, through the root system that reached into the limestone and the specialized fungal network that had evolved alongside it for millennia. The strike left scars—darkened wood, burned bark, resin weeping from wounds that would never fully heal. The force of the electricity restructured the cellular tissue of the root system at a microscopic level, loosening the rigid connections that bound the tree to immobility, introducing a kind of electrochemical malleability into structures that had always been designed for permanence.

And in the moment of the strike, a man who had been sheltering beneath the tree—seeking protection from the rain on a route that should have avoided the storm but had not—felt the same lightning pass through him. His hands, placed against the bark when the strike came, received the full force of the electrical burn. His body, already sensitive to the earth's electrical currents in ways that would not be understood for another thousand years, underwent a transformation that would alter the remaining centuries of his life.

The man's name was Farovald, and he was thirty-nine years old when the lightning made him something other than mortal.

He staggered away from the tree when the strike ended, his burned hands hanging useless at his sides, his body convulsing with the aftereffects of the electricity. He did not understand what had happened to him. He could not have understood it—the mechanisms were too far beyond the knowledge of his time, too deeply embedded in the biology of specialized adaptation that would only be discovered and named centuries later.

But he understood that he had been touched by something vast and terrible, that it had rewritten some essential part of him, and that whatever had happened in that moment would color the remainder of his existence in ways he could not yet begin to comprehend.

The tree, in its own way, understood much the same thing.

For two hundred years, Italus and Farovald would exist in a strange parallel existence, never truly together but fundamentally connected by the singularity of that moment. The tree would learn, very slowly, to move through the soil and stone of the Pollino. The man would learn, even more slowly, that aging had become optional, that his body would repair itself from injuries that should have been fatal, that the decades would stretch out before him in a way that no other human would ever experience.

And the secret of that moment, that shared transformation, would be kept by both of them in the only way such secrets could be kept—through silence, through concealment, through the careful management of knowledge and the deliberate construction of distance from the understanding of ordinary men.

The storm passed, as all storms do. The lightning moved on to strike other peaks, other trees, other lives that it would alter without intention or malice. The rain eased and eventually ceased. The clouds broke, and the Pollino emerged again into daylight, changed in some ways and entirely unchanged in others.

A man walked down from the mountains with burned hands and no explanation for them, and a tree began, so slowly that centuries would pass before the change became truly evident, to move.

---

Luca did not sleep much that night. He lay on his pallet in the corner of his family's small stone house and listened to the sounds of the village settling into darkness. His father's snoring from the inner room. The dogs moving restlessly in the yard. The sound of wind in the eaves, bringing with it the scent of autumn and stone and distant resin.

He understood, in the way that young people sometimes understand things without being taught them, that he had crossed some kind of threshold. That the world he inhabited before this moment—the simple world of seasons and animals and the repetitive work that filled a shepherd's days—was no longer entirely real to him. He had seen something that should not exist, and he had been told by a stranger with burned hands and old eyes that the only appropriate response was silence.

Silence and prayer.

The next morning, before his family rose, Luca went to his mother.

"I've been thinking about taking up prayer," he told her. "More seriously. The monks say God speaks more clearly in the high places."

His mother looked at him with an expression that contained both surprise and something like satisfaction. She was a woman of faith, or at least of the practical faith that one maintained in a small village where the alternative to faith was to confront the randomness and violence of existence directly.

"That's good," she said. "The monks will help you. You can go to the monastery, ask for guidance. They like young people who are serious about their faith."

His father, when told, simply grunted acknowledgment. Prayer was not something he was interested in, but it was not something he would forbid either. If his son wanted to spend time with monks and in contemplative practice, it was a respectable use of a young man's time.

And so Luca began his first practice of concealment.

He would rise early, tell his family he was going to the high pastures, and walk instead toward the monastery. Sometimes he did actually visit the monks, listening to their teachings about the nature of God and the soul and the proper way to conduct a Christian life. Mostly, though, he would turn off the main path before reaching the monastery and climb higher into the Pollino, toward the grove and the tree that was, impossibly, learning to move.

He studied the displacement patterns with the focus of a scholar, though he was no scholar. He noted the direction of movement, the speed at which the roots progressed, the way the trunk's lean shifted with the seasons. He began to understand, through close observation, something of the mechanism by which the tree accomplished its slow relocation—the way the roots that served as anchors would tighten, creating tension, then release, and the trunk would settle slightly into a new position. The resin would bleed, the roots would rest, and then the process would begin again.

He never saw Farovald again during those early years, though he became aware of being watched occasionally, a presence in the mountains that observed his observation but never made itself known. The man had given him one piece of advice, and Luca had made it his philosophy: he kept silent. He asked no questions in the village about moving trees or strange men with burned hands. He did not discuss what he saw, even with himself, except in the form of the careful records he began to keep, hidden in a small leather journal that he carried in his pack.

These records were written in a kind of shorthand, using symbols and abbreviated phrases that would mean nothing to anyone who happened to discover them. He recorded the position of the roots, the angle of the trunk's lean, the presence or absence of resin weeping. He recorded the dates, the weather, the patterns he observed. He was constructing a record of something that should not be recordable, something that existed outside the ordinary boundaries of natural law.

He was, without knowing it, beginning the practice that would define his entire life. He was becoming a guardian, taking on the responsibility of witnessing and maintaining the secret of a tree that moved and a transformation that could not be explained.

The years passed.

Luca grew older. His voice deepened. His shoulders broadened from the work of herding and climbing. His knowledge of the mountains expanded from the areas around the village to more distant peaks, more remote valleys. And all the while, the tree continued its slow progression northward, and Luca continued to watch, to record, to maintain his silence.

He never spoke of it to anyone. Not his parents, not the monks, not the other shepherd boys who occasionally ventured into the high pastures. The secret became so much a part of him that he sometimes forgot it was a secret at all. It simply became his life, one that  was a hidden life alongside the visible one, a current running beneath the surface of his days that no one else could perceive.

Until the day, many years later, when he would discover that others had been keeping the same silence, had been guarding the same secret, and that the responsibility he had assumed alone would, eventually, need to be shared.

But that was still in the future. For now, in the cool darkness of autumn, with the Pollino settling into winter and the evidence of the tree's movement hidden beneath snow that would erase the scored earth, Luca lay awake and understood that he had been chosen for something, though he did not yet understand what, or why, or for how long the burden would rest upon his shoulders.

# Italus - The Lightening Tree
## Book 1, Chapter 1

The ground told him first.

Luca noticed it on a morning in late autumn when he was thirteen, moving the sheep past the north ridge where the old pines stood. The earth under his heel had changed. Not visibly—the scattered needles lay as they always did, amber and brittle on the limestone—but the pressure of the ground answered differently. Where he had stepped a hundred times along this shepherd's trail, a finger-width of fresh soil had risen, then settled again, like flesh that had been pressed and was still remembering the shape of the touch.

He knelt and placed his palm flat against it.

The soil was cool but not cold, and beneath the coolness ran a faint vibration, so subtle it might have been his own pulse reflected back. He pulled his hand away and looked toward the tree itself.

The pine stood perhaps forty paces up the slope. It was old enough that calling it a tree felt inadequate—it was more the architecture of one, a massive trunk that had begun its slow spiral upward perhaps two centuries before Luca was born, its needles still dense and dark green along the upper crown but sparse along the lower limbs, which meant either great age or recent strain. The tree had always been there. It was the kind of landmark shepherds used to locate themselves—the Leaning Pine, though Luca had never understood why it was called that. All pines leaned something, bent by the perpetual wind that moved through the Pollino Heights.

But this one was not where it had been.

He stood and walked toward it, his gaze moving from the base of the trunk to the ground around it. The limestone was scored fresh, pale where the weathering had not yet darkened it. Root fragments lay scattered, the lighter wood of recent breaks exposed to air. The ground around the tree's base was disturbed in a pattern that made no sense at first—the soil was gouged and displaced as though something very heavy and very slow had rolled there, pressing and releasing, pressing and releasing in a rhythm like breathing.

Luca's chest tightened. He was fourteen now, old enough to work without close watching, old enough to notice when the world behaved in ways his elders had not prepared him for. He sat back on his heels and looked at the tree again.

The roots. The massive roots that had held the trunk upright against the wind had moved. The displacement pattern showed it clearly once he understood what he was seeing. The tree had not fallen. It had not broken. It had simply... shifted. Relocated. The roots had lifted from the earth, found new purchase perhaps three full paces from where they had been, and settled into the ground as though they had been waiting for this place all along.

He stood and walked slowly around the tree, noting the details with the meticulous attention that had kept him from losing sheep in the mountain passes. The resin on the northern side of the trunk was darker, as though it had wept recently and then dried to a harder consistency. The bark showed no damage. The needles responded to the wind with their normal slight tremor. Everything was intact.

Everything was alive.

What he had found was not a catastrophe but evidence of something for which he had no name.

He stayed through the afternoon, until the light began its collapse toward the ridge. He did not tell anyone. Instead, he returned the sheep to the lower pastures with excuses about needing to scout new forage higher up, then made his way back to the tree alone in the first darkness.

This became the shape of his autumn. During the day he moved the flocks and performed the tasks his family expected of him. At night, and whenever he could extract himself from observation, he climbed toward the heights. He began carrying a stick, a shepherd's staff carved and worn smooth by his grandfather, and he used it to mark the ground around the tree. Not obviously—small nicks against the limestone, pressure marks in the soil. If the tree moved again, he would know by how much and in what direction.

His mother noticed his absence. His father asked where he was going so often. His younger sister Elia followed him once and then stopped following when he was unkind about it, told her she was too slow, that the heights were dangerous, that he was old enough to be trusted but she was not. She was only eight and accepted this reasoning because it was the tone of someone who knew the mountains.

He did return to the tree. A week after his first discovery, the marks had shifted. The displacement pattern had advanced perhaps the width of a hand toward the southwest, and new resin had bled from the cambium in a line that seemed to follow the tree's rotation. He added new marks and returned three days later to find them moved again.

The tree was walking.

This knowledge settled into his chest like a stone. He did not speak it aloud. He did not write it. He simply carried it with him, this impossible fact, and arranged his life around protecting it.

By mid-winter, the pattern was clear enough that he could anticipate the next movement within a day or two. The tree moved slowly—a pace or less with each shift—and only after certain conditions were met. Heavy rain appeared to trigger movement. A particular wind direction that came down the limestone faces seemed to encourage it. But there were other variables, factors he could not parse, and this uncertainty became something he cultivated rather than resisted.

He was the only one who knew.

The thought was large enough to contain him entirely some days.

It was in the snow that fell in February that he first truly understood how singular his knowledge was. Snow collected on the displacement sites and marked them clearly for anyone who looked. But no one came this far into the heights anymore. The pilgrimage routes had shifted a generation ago, and the shepherds from the lower villages kept to safer terrain. He was alone with the tree, and the tree was moving under his sole attention, answering in its slow way to pressures and seasons and patterns that seemed written in the ground itself.

He was fashioning a new set of marks, using stones this time instead of scratches, when a voice reached him from the tree line.

"You're not praying, I think."

Luca's hands froze. He did not turn around. The voice was male, measured, carrying an accent that suggested the mountain villages higher up, or perhaps somewhere beyond them. When Luca finally turned, he found a man standing perhaps twenty paces away, half-shadowed by the pines. The man was perhaps forty, or perhaps sixty—there was something in his build that made age difficult to read. His hair was dark, threaded with gray at the temples. His hands were visible at his sides, empty and still.

"You climb here alone," the man continued. It was not a question. "Multiple times. Your marks are visible if you know how to read the ground. You're careful, but not careful enough." The man's eyes moved to the tree. "What are you looking for?"

"Shelter," Luca said, the lie emerging fast. "In case the weather turns."

"There's better shelter lower down. The ruins near the spring. You'd be out of the wind, at least." The man was still looking at the tree. "You're not a shepherd keeping lost animals from straying. I've watched how you move. You're counting something."

Luca's throat felt narrow. He could run—he knew the terrain better than this stranger did—but something in the man's stance suggested that running would be answered with pursuit, and he was already breathing hard from the work of climbing. Instead, he said nothing and waited.

"Your excuses are poor," the man said finally. "Every time someone asks why you're going into the heights, your answer changes. First it's prayer. Then it's a lost ewe. Then it's checking traps. A different lie each time means you're trying to hide something, not protect a habit." The man turned to face him directly. "What's worth lying so badly about?"

The storm came that night, moving in from the west with the speed of something alive and hunting. Luca had been heading down the slope, moving quickly because the light was failing and because the stranger had unsettled him in ways he couldn't name. The wind came first, then the rain turning to sleet, then the darkness compressing everything into a narrow space where up was just a direction of greater cold.

He sheltered in a rock outcropping he knew, the one the man had mentioned—the ruins near the spring, though he'd never thought of them as ruins before. They were just old stone, fitted without mortar in a way that suggested someone had built them a very long time ago for a purpose that was no longer remembered. The shelter was deep enough that he could fit inside it, and the mouth was narrow enough to deflect most of the wind. He waited there through the night, listening to the storm shatter itself against the rock, thinking about the stranger and his careful questions and his knowledge of marks that should have been invisible.

When the morning came, it came wrong. The air was still. The rain had stopped. But the wind had changed direction, and with it had come something else—a smell of burnt stone, of ozone, of air that had been split open and was still bleeding the memory of its splitting. Luca stepped out of the shelter and climbed toward the ridge.

The tree was wrong.

Not fallen. Not broken. But its position had shifted violently. The displacement pattern was no longer a slow, measured series of movements. It was a single massive displacement, as though the tree had been seized and twisted by something with terrible strength. The roots on the eastern side had been torn, exposing the pale wood underneath. The resin was darker than he'd ever seen it, nearly black in places, and it had bled down the trunk in thick rivulets that had hardened to a glassy state.

But what caught his attention was the scorched earth.

A line of burnt stone ran from a point perhaps fifty paces away directly to the tree's exposed roots. The limestone was blackened, cracked from the heat, and in places the surface had fractured completely, leaving gaps where ash had settled. The grass was gone. The smaller plants had been carbonized to nothing.

Lightning, Luca understood. A direct strike. So close to the tree that the energy had burned the ground black.

He climbed closer, his hands shaking. The tree's bark was intact on most of the trunk, but on the south-facing side there was a mark—a long, shallow scar that ran from the height of his head down toward the roots. The scar was still oozing resin, fresh and warm to the touch.

The tree had survived.

He should have been afraid. Instead, he knelt again and placed his hand on the warm bark, feeling the pulse of the resin, the steady presence of growth continuing beneath the damage. The tree was still alive. The tree was still moving.

The knowledge settled deeper now, past the stone in his chest, into something more fundamental.

He heard the footsteps before he saw the figure emerging from the smoke-hazed air. The same man from yesterday, moving slowly, deliberately. His hands were visible again, empty again. But there was something about him that had changed. His right hand was burned, the palm dark red and blistering. His left hand was worse—the skin had split in places, and the underlying tissue was raw and wept serum that had darkened to a crust.

"So you're the only one watching," the man said. He was breathing heavily, as though he'd run far and fast. "That's good. That's necessary. If others knew..." He trailed off, looking at Luca with eyes that seemed much older than the face containing them. "You need to be more careful. And you need to understand that what you're protecting is worth protecting."

"What's your name?" Luca asked.

"Farovald," the man said. "I was here when the storm happened. Before you were born, before your father was born. I was... nearby." He looked at his burned hands as though they belonged to someone else. "The lightning found us both. It changed us. But you're not seeing that, and you need to stay unseen for the rest of your life. Your family thinks you're odd already. Your mother mentioned it—that you wander, that you're distant, that you love the cold and the dark more than other children. Let them think that. Let them think you're praying when you come here. Prayer is something that makes sense to them. Prayer is safe."

"Did the lightning..." Luca couldn't finish the sentence. The question was too large, and he didn't have the words to contain it.

"Change me?" Farovald flexed his burned hands carefully, wincing. "Yes. But not the way you're thinking. I'm not magic. The tree isn't magic. What happened was real, which is harder than magic. It was three things at once—the lightning, the stone, the fungal networks running through the limestone like veins. They all met at the same moment, and the meeting changed the shape of what we are." He looked at the tree again. "It doesn't speak. It doesn't think the way you do. But it feels things. It knows pressure, and chemistry, and the slow patience of roots. And now it can move."

"Why?" Luca asked.

"Because it was struck while it was growing. The lightning restructured the cellular architecture. The roots aren't tendons—they're more than that now. They can articulate in ways pine roots shouldn't be able to. The tree is learning how to use them."

Farovald sat down heavily on the blackened stone. "You're going to be its guardian. I can see that already, the way you're attending to it. It will take you decades to understand what that means. The tree will probably outlive you by centuries. It will move, and you'll learn to move with it. You'll protect the knowledge of it, carry it forward, pass it to someone else when you're too old to maintain the care yourself. And the tree will do what trees do—grow, and endure, and continue."

"Why can't you do it?" Luca asked. "You were here first."

"Because I can't be what it needs. I'm temporary by comparison. I was struck in the event, yes, and I survived, and I've changed in ways that let me sense what it's doing. But I wasn't rooted. I'm still human. I still move through the world in human ways. The tree needs someone anchored in time and place. Someone who can learn the patterns." Farovald stood again, with effort. "Someone young enough to develop the habit of attention."

He turned to leave, then stopped. "Your sister. She followed you once. Don't let her come back here again. Not yet. Not until you're ready to teach her."

"How long will that be?" Luca asked.

"Years," Farovald said. "Maybe decades. Long enough that she'll have her own life, her own concerns, and you'll have to convince her that she wants this responsibility. That's the hardest part of guardianship—not the care itself, but the passing of it forward to someone who has to choose to carry it."

He moved back toward the tree line, then paused one final time. "Prayer," he said. "Use it. Tell your family you come here to pray. It's close enough to the truth that it won't feel like a lie to them, and it gives you the cover you need. The mountains are full of holy men and women seeking solitude. They'll understand prayer. They won't understand what you're actually doing."

Then he was gone, moving back into the pines with a careful, measured step that suggested his burned hands were not the only thing the lightning had damaged.

Luca remained with the tree through the morning, reading the displacement pattern, understanding that something fundamental had shifted in the night. The movement was no longer predictable. The tree had reacted to the strike with a massive repositioning, and he would have to recalibrate his observations, his marks, his understanding of what the tree needed.

He descended as the day climbed toward its zenith, telling his mother that he'd been praying in the heights, that the thunder had frightened him but he was safe. She believed him because he looked frightened, and he was—though not of the thunder. She served him bread and cheese without comment, understanding only that her strange boy had sought comfort in the old ways, and that was good. That was normal, even if nothing else about him was.

That night, as he lay in the darkness of the stone house, listening to the wind in the eaves, Luca understood what Farovald had meant about guardianship. It wasn't a burden that could be carried lightly. It was the kind of knowledge that changed the shape of everything—your family, your work, your place in the village. It was a secret that would require him to construct a life around protecting it, to become someone who could move through the world with patience and attention, noticing patterns that others would never see, marking time in a way that served something older and stranger than himself.

The tree would continue to move. He would continue to return. His life had already begun its long reorientation toward a task he'd never known existed three days before.

But that knowledge was his alone now. His to carry, his to develop, his to eventually pass forward to someone else—someone who would stand in the same place he stood now, kneeling in the cold, learning to read the language of displaced earth and living wood and the endless patience of a tree that had learned, against all probability, how to walk.

# Chapter 1

The ground told stories to those who knew how to read them.

Luca knelt at the base of the ancient olive, his weathered fingers tracing the pale scored marks where soil had been churned fresh. Two weeks prior, he had last visited this grove in the high Pollino, and the earth beneath Italus had been undisturbed—the same hard-packed, mineral-rich floor he had known for months. Now, the tree's massive root system had shifted. Not dramatically; the displacement was measured in finger-widths, in the barely perceptible cant of trunk against sky. But real. Unmistakable to anyone who paid attention, and Luca had paid attention to very little else since the spring.

He sat back on his heels, studying the scored crescent where bark-rough roots had scraped downward through resistant soil. The tree had moved. Or been moved. The distinction mattered, though he could not quite articulate why.

The wind crossed the high plateau in long, steady sweeps, carrying the smell of limestone dust and the sharper herbal note of sage growing between the stones. It was early autumn—September, deep into the year 789—and the Pollino uplands lay mostly empty. Shepherds came in spring and summer; monks from the monastery at Rossano occasionally ventured this far inland, though their path was lower, threading the river valleys. Luca had encountered none of them here. He came alone.

He always came alone.

The olive was immense, its trunk easily four men in girth, its crown spreading wide enough to cast shadow over a full half-acre when the sun was high. Local tradition held it was ancient when the Romans passed through, which made it somewhere between five hundred and a thousand years old—a measure of time that meant nothing to Luca except that the tree had been growing and living through wars and kingdoms and the slow accretion of centuries before he was born. It did not look dead. Nothing about it suggested disease or decline. But three seasons ago, Luca had begun to suspect that something about the tree was not entirely ordinary.

He reached out and pressed his palm against the bark. It was warm from the afternoon sun, rough with the texture of a millennium's accumulated scarring. He closed his eyes.

Nothing happened. Nothing ever happened when he touched it directly. The revelation, if it could be called that, came instead through observation: the subtle wrongness of light through the canopy, the way the branches did not quite follow the geometry that surrounding oaks and pines obeyed, the peculiar depth of the shadow it cast—sometimes shorter than the angle of the sun should allow, sometimes longer. Small things. The accumulation of small things.

He opened his eyes and withdrew his hand.

In the distance, where the plateau dropped away toward lower elevation, he could see the brown-green patchwork of the inland valleys, the thread of the Coscile River catching white glints where it ran shallow. Beyond that lay Rossano, the monastery where a small community of monks maintained a scriptorium and a library. Luca knew three of them by face and name: Brother Damiano, who kept the herb garden and had a scholar's careful attention to detail; Brother Tomás, who had traveled in Spain and France before taking vows; and Brother Farovald, who had arrived approximately a year ago and whose origins no one seemed entirely certain about.

Farovald was the one who knew this grove.

Luca had never expected to encounter another human being at this height and distance from the monastery. He had discovered the tree through months of solitary exploration, a circuit that had become obsessive only slowly, so gradually that he had not fully recognized the pattern until the pattern was already written into his body: the way his feet knew the path without his mind directing them, the way his hand reached for the staff before dawn even registered.

Then, two months ago, he had arrived at the grove to find someone already here.

The man was old—or seemed old, though something in the way he moved suggested otherwise. He wore the gray wool of a Rossano monk, and his palms, when he had finally turned to acknowledge Luca's presence, bore marks that looked like ancient burns: silvered scar tissue following patterns that Luca had never quite seen before. Patterns almost like the branching of lightning.

"You come here often," Farovald had said. Not a question.

"I do," Luca had replied. He had seen no reason to dissemble.

"The tree interests you."

Again, not quite a question. Farovald had been looking at Italus then—the name Luca did not yet know, had not been given until much later—with an expression that encompassed something between recognition and sorrow.

"Yes," Luca said.

"There are reasons," Farovald told him. "Good reasons to pay it attention. But reasons are not answers. And answers, in this case, are not gifts I can give." He had paused, then added: "Prayer helps. If anyone asks, tell them you came here to pray. It is sufficient cover for most kinds of truth."

After that, they had seen each other perhaps a dozen times. Farovald came to the grove less frequently than Luca did, perhaps once every six or eight days, and there was a pattern to his visits that Luca had begun to track without quite understanding why he was tracking it. The monk always came in the late afternoon. He always spent time with his hand on the bark. And he always seemed to be confirming something—checking the tree's state, taking a measurement Luca could not perceive.

Which was why the root displacement troubled Luca now. It was deliberate, he was almost certain. The tree had not simply slipped; it had moved with purpose, or been moved. The direction of the disturbance suggested the roots had driven deeper into the earth, and the bark was freshly grazed in places, as if something had scraped raw the protective coating.

Luca rose to his feet and circled the tree, examining the full extent of the damage. His mind was working through possibilities that he had no framework to contain: the idea that a tree could move itself was absurd, yet the evidence was literal and physical. The idea that someone else had moved it was only slightly less absurd, given the size and mass involved.

Unless Farovald knew.

The thought arrived with a clarity that made Luca's breath catch. Farovald always seemed to know more than he should. The monk's knowledge of Luca's visits, for instance—the easy certainty with which he had announced the pattern. And his hands, those scarred palms with their branching, lightning-like marks.

Luca stood for a long time, regarding the scored earth. The light was beginning to shift toward evening, the angle of sun growing shallower. He should start back down the mountain before full dark. But something held him in place, a need to understand what he was looking at, to reconcile the physical fact of the root displacement with any rational explanation the world might offer.

The wind came again, stronger this time, and the olive's branches moved in response. For just a moment, the canopy seemed to ripple with something more than the ordinary mechanics of wind and leaf. It was the kind of moment that lasted barely long enough to register, so quick that questioning it afterward felt like questioning a dream. Yet Luca was certain he had seen it: a gathering of light in the branches, a concentration of energy that resembled nothing so much as the instant before lightning strikes.

He found himself walking.

The path downslope was the same path he always took, but today it led him not directly toward the lower valleys but instead along a ridge trail that eventually branched toward Rossano. The monastery sat in a fold of hillside, its stone buildings arranged in the orderly geometry that monastic tradition favored. Luca had visited three or four times in the two months since his first encounter with Farovald. The monks were not unwelcoming to visitors, though the community was small and its focus inward-turned. Brother Damiano, the herbalist, had offered him bread and dried figs on one visit. Brother Tomás had engaged him in conversation about the books being copied in the scriptorium. And Farovald had always seemed unsurprised by his arrival, as if he had been expecting Luca all along.

It was late in the afternoon when Luca reached the monastery gate. The community was observing the office of None—the midday prayer that the monks conducted in the late afternoon, their schedule calibrated to the work of their day. He could hear them through the open door of the small chapel, their voices in Latin following the chanted ritual. Luca waited, standing in the courtyard with its dry fountain and its orderly beds of herbs growing in geometric pattern.

Brother Damiano emerged first, his sturdy frame moving with the deliberate pace of age and routine. His face creased into a smile of recognition.

"Luca. You have come again. Good. Come, there is bread still warm, and the wine is not terrible this year. Tell me—how do you find the high country? Does it suit your temperament?"

"It does," Luca said. It was true, though incomplete. He allowed himself to be drawn into the monastery and seated at the table in the common room. Damiano brought bread and cheese, a small bowl of figs, and wine in a plain clay cup. Luca ate what was offered, understanding that to refuse would be to invite questions he was not yet prepared to answer.

"You visit that part of the plateau often," Damiano said. It was not posed as inquiry, but information. "Brother Farovald mentioned that he has seen you there."

Luca's hand paused in the act of bringing bread to his mouth. "He spoke of me?"

"Only in passing. He observed that you seemed to have found a place that called to you. He suggested that this was not a common trait in younger men. Most of your age are restless, searching. He said you seemed to be looking for something specific." Damiano smiled mildly. "Or someone. Though I may have misunderstood his meaning."

"I came to pray," Luca said, drawing on Farovald's instruction. "There is a place that seems suited to contemplation."

"Yes," Damiano said. "Brother Farovald suggested as much. He seemed to approve. Our order does not often encounter people who seek such solitude in their faith. It is a valuable thing." He drank from his own cup. "Do you ever feel that the high places contain something the lowlands lack? An emptiness that the soul recognizes?"

Before Luca could answer, another figure emerged from the corridor leading to the chapel. It was Farovald.

The monk was taller than Luca remembered, or perhaps Luca had simply forgotten the full measure of his height. He was thin without appearing fragile, and his face bore the weathering of someone who spent considerable time exposed to sun and wind. His hair was gray, receding somewhat from a broad forehead. When his eyes met Luca's, there was something in them that communicated: understanding, warning, and a quality that Luca could not name but recognized as ancient.

"Luca has come to visit us," Damiano said, with the ease of someone making an obvious social announcement.

"I see," Farovald replied. His gaze did not leave Luca. "Brother Damiano, I wonder if I might speak with our guest privately. There is a question I have been meaning to ask him, concerning the eastern approach to the plateau. I am thinking of exploring that direction myself, and I wanted his observations."

It was a thin pretext, and Damiano seemed to recognize it as such. But monastic tradition held space for quiet private conversations. Damiano nodded, gathered the remains of the meal, and withdrew toward the kitchen quarters.

Farovald sat at the table, across from Luca, and for a long moment he did not speak. When he did, his voice was very quiet.

"Something has changed," he said. Not a question.

"The tree," Luca said. "Its roots have moved. I found them displaced this afternoon."

Farovald closed his eyes. The expression on his face was complex—sadness, certainly, but also something that might have been resignation. His scarred palms lay flat on the table, and Luca found himself staring at them again: those pale, branching patterns that suggested lightning and heat.

"You have been very diligent in your visits," Farovald said, opening his eyes. "More diligent than most would be."

"What is it?" Luca asked. "The tree. What is it?"

"That," Farovald replied slowly, "is not a question I can answer directly. Not yet. Perhaps not ever, depending on circumstances I cannot predict. But I can tell you that your observation is correct. The tree moves. It has always moved. And the movement means that something is changing."

"Changing how?"

"In ways that are not yet clear," Farovald said. "But I can tell you this: your instinct to come here today, to verify what you had noticed—that instinct was sound. The tree is aware of your presence. And awareness, in this case, is a form of communication."

The words made no logical sense, and yet something in Luca recognized their truth. He remembered the moment when the canopy had seemed to ripple, when light had gathered before subsiding. He remembered the pattern of the root displacement, deliberate and directed.

"Will you tell me what happened?" Luca asked. "In the past, I mean. Something happened to the tree. Something that left a mark. I can feel it."

Farovald stood, moved to the window that looked out over the monastery courtyard toward the inland valleys. His silhouette against the fading afternoon light seemed very still, very contained.

"There was a storm," he said. "A long time ago. Two hundred years or more. Not the kind of storm that passes quickly, but something deeper, something that the sky itself could barely contain." He paused. "I was there."

And then, in the space between one heartbeat and the next, the scene shifted.

---

The mountain burned.

Not with fire, but with light—white, bright, absolute light that scraped the sky from rim to horizon. Thunder followed, but it was not sound alone; it was pressure, resonance, the earth itself shaking as if in response to a blow struck from heaven. Rain fell sideways, driven horizontal by wind that seemed to emanate from all directions at once, and the olive tree—massive even then, even two hundred years younger—twisted in the assault like something alive and terrified.

Farovald stood with his back against the trunk, his palms pressed flat against the bark, and he could feel the tree's terror, its response to the singular energy that was tearing downward from the sky. Lightning was seeking ground, seeking the earth. It followed the paths of greatest conductivity, and the olive, standing alone on the exposed plateau, was a beacon.

The man's hands burned. He felt it clearly—not pain, not yet, but the sensation of being scoured, of skin and flesh and the intricate architecture of bone being remade in the image of current and heat. The lightning came like a spear, striking through the crown of the tree and down through the trunk and into the earth below, and Farovald felt it pass through him like a door opening in his own body.

The smell of resin and burning cambium, the sharp ozone reek of superheated wood, the taste of copper on his tongue.

When the light faded, he was still standing. His palms were scorched, the skin blackened and split. His breath came in shudders. The tree swayed, its crown ravaged, branches stripped of leaves and bark. And beneath his hands, he could feel something like recognition—the tree knowing him, accepting him, binding itself to him in a way that had no name in any language he possessed.

---

Luca gasped.

He was back in the monastery's common room. The light from the window was the light of ordinary evening, and Farovald stood very still, his hands still outstretched as if they still felt the burn of that ancient moment.

"You were there," Luca said. It was not a question.

"I was," Farovald replied.

"But that was—"

"Yes," Farovald said softly. "Two hundred years. And the scars remain because some damage reaches deep enough that healing is not forgetting. The tree and I share something that began in that storm. It is not something I can explain to you, and I am telling you only because you have proven worthy of partial truth." He turned from the window. "The tree moves because it is alive in ways that trees are not ordinarily alive. And it is aware of you because you have paid attention where most people see only wood and age."

"What does it want?" Luca asked.

"I do not know," Farovald said, and the honesty in his voice was absolute. "But I know that the fact of its movement, the fact that it is reaching deeper into the earth—these things suggest that something is beginning. Something that has been dormant is waking."

He moved toward the door. "Continue to visit. Continue to observe. And if anything else changes—if the tree grows or shifts further, if the light around it becomes strange—come and tell me. Can you do that?"

Luca nodded, though he understood almost nothing of what had just occurred, could not fully distinguish between the memory he had somehow experienced and the ordinary flow of time.

Farovald paused at the doorway, and Luca saw his scarred hands one final time: the branching patterns like lightning captured in flesh, pale against the monk's weathered skin.

"The high places contain something," Farovald said, echoing Damiano's words from minutes earlier. "And the tree is at the heart of it. Pay attention. Everything that matters begins with attention."

Then he was gone, returning to the evening office, leaving Luca alone with bread and cheese and the profound certainty that his life had just divided into before and after, with no bridge between the two.
