The roar of the storm had filled everything—sky and stone and bone—two hundred years before Luca was born. Lightning had split the Pollino peaks in 589, and in that moment the mountain had changed two men forever.

Farovald remembered the singular clarity of that strike. The bolt had descended not as separate light and sound but as a unified force that arrived all at once, without warning or mercy. It had found him on the exposed ridge where he stood watching the weather turn, and the impact had driven him to his knees with a violence that seemed to reorder his understanding of what the body could endure. His palms had taken the worst of it. The lightning had entered through his upraised hands as he stood with arms raised toward the peaks, whether in prayer or defiance or simply because he had been standing that way when the sky opened, he no longer quite remembered. The burns had healed into scarred, silvered patterns that marked his skin like a map of that instant of transformation. The pain had been absolute. The aftermath had been stranger still.

Italus had been there. The lightning had altered him too, though not in any way that left visible marks. The shared singularity of that storm—the way it had bound two separate experiences into something neither could fully explain—had created a knowledge between them that required no words. Farovald carried the memory of that moment as a scar. Italus carried it differently, and the difference was precisely why Farovald had left the monastery and come back to the Pollino nearly two centuries later.

The memory released him, and Luca's present rushed back in.

The boy stood above the disturbed ground with his shoulders braced, as if preparing for another impact, though the sky was clear and the air held only the ordinary wind of the high places. The roar of the 589 storm faded to silence, leaving behind a quiet so complete it seemed unnatural. Luca's eyes were fixed downward, tracking the scored earth beneath his feet.

The ground had been worked deliberately. Someone had moved through this place recently and had not bothered to disguise the evidence, or had believed the evidence would mean nothing to anyone who might find it. The soil was darker where it had been turned. Grass that should have been established was matted and broken. A tree that had occupied this position for as long as Luca could map the terrain in his mind was gone.

He paced the space with the precision of someone who had walked this ground many times before. Twelve strides from the broken stone marker to the spot where the pine should have stood. Eight strides perpendicular, adjusting for the slope. His boots displaced loose soil with each step, and he could see where recent disturbance had cut through the weathered surface crust. Someone larger than himself had passed this way. Someone—or something—heavy enough to press deep into ground that should have resisted casual passage.

Luca's mind constructed a map of the absence. The tree had been substantial. A pine old enough to have grown in a particular configuration, one that he had used for orientation on his climbs. He could recall the angle of its primary branches, the way it had cast shadow on certain afternoons, the precise juncture where he had once scraped his shoulder on rough bark. And now that tree was gone, and in its place was only turned earth and the beginning of new confusion.

He crouched at the edge of the disturbance, running his fingers across the broken ground. The soil was still loose. Rain had not yet settled it. This work had been done recently enough that the disorder remained stark. Days, perhaps. Not weeks. The calculation made his chest tighten.

Italus had moved.

The certainty arrived with more force than he expected. Luca's hands pressed against the earth, and the ground seemed to tilt. The valley below blurred. His vision contracted to the immediate space around his fingers, where disturbed soil gave way to the intact ground beyond. The mountain was doing something to the air at this altitude, making it thin and difficult to parse. Or perhaps it was only that the landscape had rearranged itself, and his mind could not quite accept that the map he had constructed through careful observation and repeated passage had become unreliable.

He straightened, forcing his breath to steady. There was no reason for the vertigo. He was accustomed to the heights. His family had lived in these mountains for generations. The thin air, the steep pitches, the sense of standing above the world—all of this was familiar. But familiarity and understanding were not the same thing. He understood the Pollino's geography in the way a cartographer understands a territory he has charted, but he was beginning to understand that the territory had not remained still to be charted.

The scored ground extended in a direction that suggested movement down the slope and toward the eastern exposure. Luca traced the disturbance with his eyes, reading the pattern as someone else might read written text. The pressure and pattern of disruption suggested weight and purpose. The figure—the thing, he was not yet ready to name it—had traveled with deliberate intent. Not fleeing. Not wandering. Moving toward something or away from something, with knowledge of the ground and the direction.

He straightened and began to follow the trail.

The break in the disturbed earth became more subtle as he descended. The ground flattened, and the vegetation became denser. Where the tree had been, the passage had been obvious. Here, the evidence suggested itself in negative form. Grass that should have been upright was slightly bent. Lichen-covered stones had been moved. A small shrub bore the mark of something substantial passing close to it, a bruising on the foliage that would heal within weeks.

Luca's mind worked through the implications. He had been coming to the Pollino for months now. Weekly, and sometimes more frequently. His family had begun to ask questions about the nature of these climbs. His mother had suggested that perhaps his devotion to prayer had begun to border on obsession. His father, more direct, had noted that shepherds did not spend so much time on the high ridges during the lambing season.

They did not know, and Luca had developed a practiced skill at deflection. He told them that he needed solitude. He told them that the mountains helped him think clearly. He told them that the community priest had encouraged extended retreat. All of these things were technically true, though none captured the full truth. The full truth was something he could not explain without sounding mad.

The full truth was that something had come to the Pollino heights and had left evidence of its presence, and Luca had seen that evidence. He had found the place where Italus had rested, the depression in the earth that corresponded to no animal he knew, the marks on rock that suggested intent and consciousness. And when he had brought his priest to show him, the old man had examined the site and had said nothing, had looked at Luca with an expression of profound sadness, and had told him to keep away from the high places.

The priest's refusal to acknowledge what they had both seen had been the moment when the climate of Luca's life had shifted fundamentally. Before that moment, he had believed that adults understood the world and would provide explanation. After that moment, he had understood that adults sometimes saw things they did not wish to acknowledge.

So Luca had returned alone.

He had returned every week, and sometimes more than that, and each time he had found new evidence. Not much. A mark on stone. A pattern in the earth. A scent in the wind that suggested passage. The thing that moved through the Pollino did not leave obvious tracks. It moved with care, with awareness of concealment. But it was large, and it was present, and it was not moving deeper into the wilderness.

It was moving toward the village.

The implications of that trajectory had driven Luca's recent obsession. If the creature, the entity, the impossible presence was migrating downslope, then eventually it would reach habitation. Eventually it would encounter other people. Eventually it would be seen, and then the pretense that it was a matter for solitude and prayer would shatter entirely.

That was why he had come again today, despite the questions, despite the suspicion. He needed to understand the rate of its movement. He needed to construct a map of its passage. He needed to know when it would reach a point where his secret keeping became untenable.

He crouched again at a point where the disturbance seemed to orient toward the lower slope. The trail was becoming harder to read. The creature—Italus, he could acknowledge the name now if only in his own mind—had learned to move more carefully, or perhaps these older marks were simply less distinct.

A shadow fell across the ground.

Luca straightened, and the world reassembled itself. He was no longer alone on the high ridge.

The man was older, thin in the particular way of someone who had spent years in sparse mountains. He wore the rough wool of a monk's habit, patched and faded. His face was weathered to the color of old leather, and his eyes held the peculiar clarity of someone looking at something far away even when his gaze was direct.

"You come here often," the man said. It was not a question.

Luca's initial impulse was to flee. The stranger had appeared without warning, approaching from a direction Luca had not seen. The skill required to move unheard on this terrain was not trivial. The fact that the man had achieved it suggested capabilities that aligned uneasily with Luca's current state of heightened suspicion.

"I pray," Luca said. The lie came easily by now, though it still felt hot in his mouth.

"You pray very thoroughly," the stranger said. "And you pray with your eyes on the ground. That suggests you are searching for something to pray about, rather than praying about something you already know. What do you search for in the earth?"

Luca did not answer. The man was watching him with an intensity that suggested he expected silence. He was dressed as a monk, but there was nothing monastic about the way he stood. His posture held tension. His hands, which hung at his sides, bore old scarring on the palms. The scarring was extensive, the kind that suggested severe burn or lightning damage. The skin had healed into silvered patterns that caught the mountain light.

"My name is Farovald," the man said. "I have lived in the high places for a long time. I notice patterns. Repetitions. Things that suggest intention beneath their surface. And I have noticed you. Coming, returning, searching. Your excuses for these journeys are weak. Your family does not believe them. The village speaks of it."

"I don't know what you mean," Luca said. His voice was steadier than he felt.

"Then let me be more direct," Farovald said. "You come here searching for evidence of something. You tell your family you come for prayer. But you do not pray. You examine the ground. You measure distances. You trace patterns. And you have become reckless enough that your behavior is drawing attention from people who will not let the matter rest."

The accuracy of this assessment was startling. Luca's mind raced through possibilities. The stranger could not know about Italus. No one could know about Italus. The whole purpose of these expeditions was to maintain secrecy about the presence on the mountain.

Unless Farovald knew for a different reason.

"Who are you?" Luca asked.

"I told you. A monk. A hermit of the high places. I came to the Pollino seeking solitude and found something else. Something that changed my understanding of what the world contains. And now I watch, and I wait, and I observe people like you who come searching for the same thing I came to understand."

Luca's throat was tight. "There is nothing here to find."

"Then why do you search?" Farovald moved closer. He did not move like a threat. He moved like someone settling into a position of conversation. "And do not waste more lies. We are past that now. The question is not whether you search for something extraordinary. The question is what you intend to do when you find it, and how much longer you can maintain this pretense without bringing down the attention of the entire valley."

"I don't know what I'm looking for," Luca said. It was the first true thing he had said in this conversation. "I'm trying to understand what came to this place."

"And what have you concluded?"

"That it's still here. That it's moving. That eventually someone will notice besides me."

Farovald nodded, as if this assessment confirmed something he had already known. "You have perhaps two weeks before the village consensus becomes that you are either disturbed or up to something they need to investigate. After that, your private expeditions become public knowledge, and public knowledge in a place like this quickly becomes public action. People will organize. People will search. And if they search with intent, they will find evidence that the young scholar comes to the high places looking for tracks of something unusual."

"So what do you suggest?" Luca asked.

"Prayer," Farovald said. "Genuine prayer. Formal retreat. You tell your mother and father that you have experienced a spiritual calling. You tell them that you intend to spend extended time in the high places in religious contemplation. You ask their permission and their blessing. The village priest will support this narrative because it flatters the church's influence over the young people. Your family will approve because it locates your behavior within a framework they understand. And you will have justification for your presence here that cannot be questioned."

Luca considered this. The strategy was sound. The church did encourage retreat and contemplation, particularly in young people who showed inclination toward spiritual questions. The priest certainly would support the narrative. And his parents, while concerned about his behavior, would accept the framing as legitimate.

"And what do I do when I'm here?" Luca asked. "When I'm supposedly praying?"

"You pay attention," Farovald said. "You develop the habits of careful observation. You learn to see without being obvious about the seeing. You begin to understand the patterns of movement and passage. You prepare yourself."

"Prepare for what?"

Farovald was quiet for a long moment. His scarred hands turned upward slightly, as if examining something invisible in the palm lines.

"For what comes when observation becomes insufficient," he said finally. "But that is a lesson for later. For now, you need to secure your access to this place. The prayer framework gives you that. Use it."

Luca wanted to ask more, but something in Farovald's expression suggested the conversation was ending. The monk began to move back the way he had come, or perhaps not the way he had come. His movement seemed to follow lines of terrain that Luca would not have chosen.

"Wait," Luca said. "How did you know? About the village? About my excuses?"

Farovald did not turn, but he paused. "Because I have watched patterns on these mountains for a very long time. I know how they break and reform. I know what disruption looks like when it approaches from outside the established order. And I know what it looks like when someone young begins to see things that change their understanding of the world they thought they knew. I recognize it because I have been what you are becoming."

He moved then, and within moments he was gone, disappearing into the folds of terrain as completely as if the mountain had absorbed him.

Luca stood alone on the ridge above the disturbed ground where Italus had passed. The afternoon light was beginning to shift. He had perhaps three hours before the descent back to the village would become difficult. Three hours to decide whether the stranger had offered genuine advice or a subtle trap.

But Farovald was right about one thing. The village was noticing. His mother's questions had become more pointed. The shepherd who occasionally passed the lower paths had begun to watch him with new interest. The balance between private investigation and public suspicion was shifting, and Luca understood that he could not maintain the current equilibrium much longer.

Prayer was a framework that made sense to everyone around him. Prayer was something that the church encouraged, that families supported, that the community understood as legitimate. Prayer would provide him with cover for his continued presence on the high places, and it would do so without attracting the kind of organized investigation that would destroy everything.

He turned back toward the village, carrying the decision with him. Tomorrow he would approach his parents with humility and apparent spiritual hunger. Tomorrow he would ask for their permission to undertake regular retreat and contemplation. Tomorrow he would transform his desperate search for a truth no one wanted to acknowledge into something his family and his community could celebrate.

The foundation of his guardianship had been laid in that moment on the ridge. Not through appointment or formal acknowledgment. Not through any agreement with Farovald or with anyone else. But through the simple choice to create a framework that allowed him to remain close to what needed watching. The lie had become a structure. The structure had become a practice. And practice, Luca was beginning to understand, was the first step toward something deeper.

He did not know yet what that something was. He did not know how much the stranger knew or why he had appeared with such perfectly calibrated advice. He did not know what the 589 storm had done to Farovald's scarred palms or why the monk seemed to know about Italus's movements as precisely as Luca did.

But he knew that he would return tomorrow. He knew that he would kneel in the chapel and pray with genuine intensity, not for God's attention but for his parents' approval. He knew that the Pollino would accept him then in a way it had not before, because he would have given himself permission to be there through the only language his community understood.

And somewhere on these mountains, something watched. Not Luca. Not anymore. Now something watched Farovald watching Luca, and all of them watched Italus moving slowly downslope toward a confrontation that none of them fully understood but all of them, in their own way, were preparing for.

# Chapter 1

The ground was wrong.

Luca's boot heel struck the earth twice, each contact sharper and deeper than memory suggested they should be. The slope here had altered, eroded downward by something purposeful and heavy, scored in parallel lines that caught the afternoon light. His stomach tightened. He crouched, running his palm across the disturbed soil, feeling the sharp edges of recently exposed stone.

This wasn't rain damage. Rain didn't move in such deliberate patterns.

He rose and turned slowly, orienting himself by the outcropping of darker rock to the east and the sentinel stone near the village route. His eyes traced the familiar slope, counting the distance, measuring the relationship between landmarks he'd memorized over weeks of careful return visits. The space held a wrongness he couldn't quite name at first. Then it became clear.

The pine was gone.

Not fallen. Not recently pruned. The evidence lay scattered: a section of root still clinging to the soil, drag marks through the loose stone, and a gap in the tree line where its mass should have broken the skyline. The old pine that had stood at this precise location for as long as the village records mentioned it, the one he'd used as a fixed point in his mental mapping of Italus's domain, had been deliberately removed.

His breath came shallow. Someone had been here. Recently. Someone strong enough to uproot or fell a mature tree and methodical enough to clean away most of the evidence of doing so. Luca closed his eyes and felt the spatial world tilt slightly. The vertigo came suddenly, a wave of disorientation that made his surroundings feel unstable, as though the very ground beneath the Pollino peaks had shifted in ways he couldn't calculate.

The sensation passed. He steadied himself and forced his mind to work through the problem methodically. The disturbance pattern suggested movement from the higher elevation downslope, toward the passes that led deeper into the hidden terrain. Italus had moved. After weeks of what Luca had believed were stationary positions, the creature had relocated entirely.

But something else surfaced in his mind as he stood there, something triggered by the physicality of the evidence before him. A memory that wasn't quite his own, though it had been grafted into his understanding somehow. Or perhaps it was something more immediate than a memory, something that lived in his blood.

---

**The storm came in 589.**

Lightning split the sky above the Pollino peaks with a roar that turned the world white. The crack didn't follow the usual rules of thunder and flash. Instead, the light and sound arrived together, as though the storm had abandoned the distance between cause and effect entirely. The air itself seemed to burn.

Two figures stood exposed on the high ridge where few creatures ventured. One was already ancient when the empire crumbled, a form of such concentrated solidity that the lightning seemed to deliberately seek him out. The other was younger, caught in the act of turning to flee, his monk's robe whipping around him like a flag caught in a maelstrom.

The lightning found both of them.

It was not an ordinary strike. The singularity of the storm, the precise convergence of the electrical fury, seemed to choose them both simultaneously, as though the phenomenon itself possessed intention. The impact came not as a bolt but as a presence, searing through skin and bone and the deeper structures that even fire could not ordinarily touch. The pain was absolute and dimensionless. It unmade the world.

Afterward, there was burning. Burning that continued long after the storm had passed, burning that lived in the palms and in the spine, burning that altered something fundamental in the relationship between body and the world's electrical skin. The monk crawled across the scorched ground, his hands blistered and blackened, and found the other figure still standing. Impossibly standing, as though the lightning had simply passed through him and left him transformed rather than destroyed.

---

The memory dissolved. Luca gasped, pressing his hand to his temple. He had never been to the Pollino peaks in 589. He had never stood in any storm like that. The knowledge was impossibly specific, more intimate than any memory could be, and it carried with it the sharp phantom of old pain, the echo of lightning that had touched skin that wasn't his own.

He forced himself to breathe normally and return his attention to the ground before him. The marks here were recent, made within days. He could read that much. What he couldn't read was the identity of whatever had made them, or the precise nature of the force that had dragged such a massive tree away from its position.

Except he could. He knew exactly what had made these marks. Italus had moved. The knowledge was certainty itself, sitting in his mind with the same weight as the impossible storm memory.

Luca began to pace, measuring out the distance from the uprooted pine to the nearest visible disturbance point, trying to establish a pattern. His legs felt unsteady, and his mind kept sliding sideways from the spatial calculations he was attempting. Each time he tried to add the measurements together, to construct a coherent map of Italus's recent position and direction, the vertigo returned. His inner ear seemed to be out of alignment with the actual slope of the ground.

He forced himself to continue. The pattern that emerged, reluctantly, showed movement toward the northern passes. Away from the lower elevations. Away from the village routes and the places where a shepherd boy might reasonably claim to be searching for lost lambs or gathering mountain herbs. This was deeper. This was the kind of retreat that would require better excuses than he'd managed so far.

His excuses were already wearing thin.

The previous five visits to these heights had been increasingly difficult to justify. The first had been easy enough. A lamb had actually gone missing, and the search had been legitimate. The second visit, he'd claimed to be looking for the same lost animal, extending the search into unlikely territory. By the fourth visit, his uncle had begun asking pointed questions about why the lamb remained missing but Luca felt compelled to return to this particular stretch of mountainside daily. By the fifth, his mother had started to watch him with an expression he couldn't quite name, something that combined suspicion with a concern deeper than his wandering alone should have provoked.

This discovery, the proof that Italus had moved, changed the situation entirely. Luca couldn't simply come back tomorrow with another flimsy excuse. He needed to establish a pattern of return visits that his family would accept without question. He needed a reason so solid that it would bear repeated scrutiny, something that wouldn't prompt questions or searches or the involvement of village authorities.

As he stood there among the scattered evidence of Italus's relocation, Luca found himself mentally cataloging the possibilities. Nothing sufficiently credible came to mind. A boy his age could claim to be herding animals, gathering herbs, seeking lost property, or aiding an elder with work in the high pastures. But each of these excuses had a limited shelf life. They could be used once, perhaps twice. After that, the village would begin to wonder why the task remained incomplete, or why the resource he claimed to be gathering had proven so elusive.

He needed something with more permanence. Something that would account for repeated visits across weeks, perhaps months. Something that wouldn't require him to produce results, only intention.

He was still considering these constraints, turning the problem over in his mind with a concentration that blocked out the normal mountain sounds, when he became aware of another presence on the slope.

The figure emerged from the upper tree line without apparent urgency, moving with the practiced ease of someone accustomed to rough terrain. He wore a monk's robe of the austere type, heavily patched and stained with the dust of the high passes. His head was uncovered, revealing dark hair touched with white, and his face carried the weathered look of a man who had spent decades in exposure to sun and wind. But it was his hands that drew Luca's attention first. Even at a distance, even in the shifting light of the late afternoon, Luca could see that the palms and fingers carried marks that weren't quite normal scarring.

The old monk descended the slope with a deliberate pace, neither hurrying nor pausing. He seemed to be approaching Luca directly, which was unusual in itself. The mountain monks who occasionally passed through the region were typically solitary and avoided conversation. Luca felt his body tense, though he couldn't have articulated a clear reason for the response.

The monk came to a stop about five paces away, his expression neutral, his eyes sharp enough that Luca felt he was being assessed with considerable precision. When the monk spoke, his voice was rough from disuse, but there was intelligence in it and something else that Luca couldn't quite identify.

"You've been here many times recently," the monk said. It wasn't a question.

Luca's throat tightened. "I'm searching for a lost lamb."

The monk's eyes moved briefly to the disturbed ground, then back to Luca's face. "The lamb is not the reason you return to this place."

There was no hostility in the statement, merely a factual observation. But it left Luca with no clear answer. He could insist on the lamb story, but something in the monk's gaze suggested that the lie would be noted and dismissed. The alternative was to tell the truth, which was impossible. There was no truth he could tell that wouldn't either expose his purpose entirely or sound like the fabrication of a desperate boy.

"I come here to think," Luca said finally, which was at least partially honest. "The heights are quiet."

The monk nodded slowly, as though this answer satisfied some internal criterion. He shifted his weight slightly, and in that small movement, Luca caught another glimpse of his palms, marked in patterns that suggested old damage from heat or electricity rather than the normal scarring of physical labor.

"The village will expect explanations," the monk said. "Your absences are being noted. Within days, perhaps a week, someone will follow you to discover what you're truly seeking." He paused, allowing this prediction to settle. "They will find no lost lamb and no logical reason for your presence here. Questions will follow."

Luca felt a spike of panic. The monk was right. He'd been negligent about the social implications of his repeated visits. The village was small, and absences were always noticed. His excuses had been wearing thin before he'd even left his home.

"What would you suggest?" Luca heard himself ask.

The monk's expression didn't change, but something shifted in his posture, a subtle softening. "Prayer," he said. "You come here to pray. The heights draw you for spiritual reasons. The solitude aids your devotion, and the specific location is sacred to you for reasons you keep private. This explanation requires no evidence. No one will ask you to produce results. The more frequently you return, the more pious you appear. The village may even celebrate your dedication."

It was brilliant in its simplicity. Luca felt the tension in his chest ease slightly as the implications unfolded in his mind. Prayer required no observable results. It couldn't fail. It was also entirely consistent with the monk's presence in the region, which lent credibility to the explanation through association. No one would question a boy who had been counseled in matters of faith by a wandering holy man.

"They'll still wonder why I choose this location," Luca said carefully.

"Then tell them that a monk has taught you there is spiritual power in the high places. That the proximity to the sky makes prayer more effective. These are things people are prepared to believe." The monk began to turn away, clearly ending the conversation. "Practice the habit of prayer here. Make it visible when others might observe. Carry something to mark the spot where you kneel. After a few weeks, your presence will become unremarkable. You will become part of the landscape."

Luca managed a small nod. "Will you come back?"

The monk paused, his gaze returning briefly to Luca's face. For a moment, something unreadable crossed his expression, something that might have been sadness or might have been recognition of a burden neither of them could avoid. "I walk these passes often. We may encounter each other again." He didn't commit to it. He only made the possibility known.

The monk continued down the slope, disappearing into the trees with the same quiet efficiency with which he'd appeared. Luca stood among the evidence of Italus's passage and felt the weight of his situation clarify. He would come back tomorrow with a blanket and something that marked the location as his place of prayer. He would make a habit of kneeling here in full view of the path. He would transform his desperate searching into a narrative of piety that the village would not question.

He was beginning the work of concealment without fully understanding what he was concealing or why. The knowledge sat in his body like a stone, present and heavy but not yet understood. He knew that Italus had moved. He knew that the old monk who had instructed him on the art of social deception carried marks that corresponded to the memory of a lightning strike two centuries old. He knew that something had changed in him during that moment on the slope, something that had pushed him past the normal boundaries of a village boy's life.

But he didn't yet know why.

He gathered his things and began the descent toward home, already constructing the story he would tell his mother about meeting a wandering monk who had offered spiritual counsel. It was the first real lie he had crafted with deliberation, and the ease of it troubled him in ways he couldn't quite name. But beneath the trouble was something else: the beginning of understanding that his life, whatever it had been before this afternoon, was not going to remain the same.

The Pollino peaks rose behind him as he descended, holding their secrets and their evidence. Somewhere in those heights, Italus had moved. Somewhere in those heights, a monk who carried the marks of an impossible storm walked the old passes. And somewhere in the villages and fields below, people were beginning to wonder why a boy in his sixteenth year kept disappearing into the mountains with excuses that grew more transparent each time he offered them.

By the time Luca reached the lower elevations, the light was failing. The mountains had turned dark and difficult to read, the same mountains that Italus had claimed as a domain, the same peaks where something ancient and powerful had been touched by lightning and changed in ways that left marks on human flesh.

Luca knew now that he would return tomorrow. He would return with blankets and the markers of prayer. He would return again after that, and again after that, drawn by something deeper than curiosity or duty. He was beginning the practice of guardianship without understanding what he was guarding or what burden might fall to him if his vigil failed.

The village lights appeared through the trees as he approached the final descent. He composed his expression and prepared the story about the monk. In the distance, somewhere beyond the boundary of the village, the mountains kept their watch.

# Chapter One

The ground beneath Luca's feet told stories he was learning to read, though the lessons came in a language of disturbance and displacement. He knelt at the edge of the scored earth, running his fingers along the ragged furrow that cut across the rocky soil where no furrow had been before. The Pollino heights held few secrets from someone who visited them as often as he did now, and this mark was impossibly fresh—raw stone still catching light where weather had not yet begun its slow work of dulling and darkening.

He traced the line backward with his eyes, following its direction down the slope toward the tree line where the sparse mountain pines gave way to denser growth below. Whatever had moved through here had done so with enough weight and force to leave a scar on terrain that seemed unforgiving to such casual marking. Luca's breath came steady as he worked, though his heart moved faster than the careful pace of his investigation warranted.

Behind him, the morning light spilled across the high country in that particular way it had in late summer, all clarity and shadow, no room for ambiguity. He could see for kilometers in three directions from this vantage, the landscape spreading like something offered up for inspection. And it was inspection he was conducting, methodical and deliberate, the way he had begun to conduct himself in this place over the past weeks.

He stood and turned slowly, taking in the familiar contours of the ridge and the areas beyond it. There, where the old pine had always marked the northern boundary of the open ground, where he had used it as a anchor point in his mental mapping of this place—nothing. The space was empty. Not cleared, exactly. Not entirely absent. But altered.

The displacement unsettled him in a way that made his chest tighten. He moved toward the spot where the tree should have been, his pace quickening despite his intention to move with deliberation. The ground there was different too, the stone arrangements subtly wrong, as though someone had rearranged the evidence of years and left it only slightly displaced from truth.

Luca began to pace, measuring distances with his stride, counting steps and then converting them into the internal calculations he had developed over weeks of obsessive attention. The old pine—he was certain it had stood here, or here, or perhaps here. The uncertainty gnawed at him. His father had brought him to these heights twice when he was younger, and Luca had marked the landscape then with the casual attention of childhood. Since his summons began, since he had felt called back to this place without understanding the calling, he had returned seventeen times. Seventeen times he had walked this ridge, and each time he had refined his mental image of its geometry, its fixed points, its markers of immutability.

Now immutability had moved.

The vertigo arrived without warning, a sensation of his internal balance shifting as though the earth beneath him had tilted in some direction only his body could perceive. Luca staggered, extending one hand, though there was nothing nearby to steady himself against. His vision swam for a moment, the vast expanse of the Pollino heights wheeling around him as though he were the center of a turning wheel rather than a figure standing still. The impossibility of the altered landscape combined with the physical sensation of his own disorientation, and for an instant he could not separate what had moved—the earth or himself.

He forced himself to stand motionless, breathing deeply, waiting for the sensation to pass. It did, receding as unexpectedly as it had arrived, leaving behind only a lingering sense of displacement that his body could not quite reconcile with what his mind was recording.

It was in that moment of stillness, as he waited for the world to settle back into proper alignment, that memory struck him with the force of something that had been waiting beneath the surface of his thoughts, patient as predator.

---

The storm had come without warning that day, or perhaps with warnings that the younger version of himself had been too naive or too distracted to read. The sky had changed color in the way the Pollino sky did when the weather rose up from the south and collided with the mountain masses, turning the air itself into something dense and charged. Luca had been younger then, not yet born probably, and yet the memory lived in him now with the vivid clarity of lived experience.

This made no sense. He had not been there. And yet—

The lightning had come down like something with intention, like a hand reaching from the clouds with purpose. Italus had been in the open ground when it struck. Luca could see him, impossibly, standing alone on the ridge with his arms at his sides, his dark robes whipping around him in the storm wind. The lightning had found him as though he were calling it down, as though they had an appointment kept across the fabric of some other understanding.

And Farovald—older then, mature already in the frame that Luca knew now, his form somehow both solid and wavering in the storm light—had stood nearer to the tree line, close enough to see but not so close as to intervene. The lightning had changed both of them in an instant. Luca could see it happen: the way Italus had taken the strike as though accepting a benediction, the way Farovald had gone utterly still in witness.

When it was over, when the lightning had released them and the storm had moved on, leaving only the smell of scorched stone and disturbed air, both of them had stood in the aftermath with something altered in their configuration. Luca could not have named what was different, but he felt the weight of transformation as though he had experienced it himself, as though the storm had marked him as much as it had marked them.

---

Luca gasped, sudden and sharp, pulling himself back to the present as though being dragged upward from deep water. The quiet of the Pollino heights rushed in around him, the ordinary daylight, the absence of storm, the simple fact of the scored earth and the missing tree. His chest heaved as though he had been running, though he had not moved.

He had not been there. That was impossible. That was a vision, or a dream that had somehow infected waking, or some trick of the mind that he did not yet understand. But the certainty of it remained, settling into his thoughts like sediment, like a fact that had arrived complete and whole and would not be dislodged by logic or reason.

He pressed his palms against his thighs, grounding himself in the physical sensation of his own body, in the solid reality of the mountain beneath his feet. The sun was bright and ordinary. The wind carried the dry smell of high-country grasses and distant pine. Nothing had changed except everything, and he was alone in this knowledge, alone with the evidence that someone or something had moved through this place recently, and alone with the impossible certainty that Italus and Farovald had stood in the fire of an ancient storm together.

Luca moved forward toward the space where the tree should have been, his investigation driven now by something more urgent than casual mapping. The ground here showed different scoring, multiple marks as though something had been dragged or moved, or as though it had rested here for a long time and then been lifted away. He knelt again, his eyes searching for details, for meaning in the arrangement of stones and the patterns of disturbance.

Whatever Italus was, wherever Italus had gone, the path of his movement was becoming legible to him. Luca had come back to these heights because something had called him back, something that lived in his blood and his bones and his breath. He had thought it was curiosity at first, the ordinary pull of a mystery that drew the mind forward. Now he wondered if it was something else entirely, something that had marked him before he was born, something that he carried in the same way that Italus and Farovald carried whatever the storm had done to them.

He looked up from the ground toward the path he had traced with his eyes, following the line of disturbance down the slope. The tree line held shadows now that the morning had progressed, and the shadows held their own kind of silence. Somewhere down there, Italus was moving, and Luca was going to follow, though following meant returning to the village with excuses that grew more thin and transparent with each repetition.

He had said he needed to walk off a troubled mind. He had said his father's livestock was straying upslope. He had said he was keeping a vow he had made to himself, a spiritual seeking that required solitude and the high places. His mother had looked at him with increasing concern, and his sister had begun to smirk at his departures, and his father had started to ask pointed questions about which vow exactly he had made and to whom.

The excuses were becoming threadbare. He could see that in the way people looked at him when he announced another expedition to the heights. The village was small enough that his repeated absences were noticed, and enough time had passed that suspicion was beginning to form. There would be consequences if he did not find a more credible reason for being here so often, if he did not construct something that his family and the broader community could accept without endless interrogation.

Luca stood, his investigation temporarily concluded. The physical evidence told him what he needed to know: Italus had moved recently, the trail was clear enough to follow if he chose to do so, and something that had been previously fixed in this landscape had been deliberately removed or relocated. More than this, he could not yet determine without moving beyond the immediate geography and into the terrain where follow-up might become obvious to observers.

He began the walk back down the slope, retracing the path he had taken up from the village, his mind divided between the practical problem of his increasingly suspicious family and the far more pressing mystery of what had happened to a creature he did not fully understand, a creature whose name had been given to him as though it were the answer to a question he had never asked.

The descent gave him time to think, and by the time he reached the lower elevations where the mountain gave way to the more populated valleys, he had begun to construct a different narrative, one that might hold up better under scrutiny. Prayer. The word arrived in his mind like a gift, like something placed there for his specific use. Prayer was a thing that could be repeated without exhaustion, that was encouraged by community, that required solitude but was not suspect. A young man praying in the high places, seeking spiritual communion, finding clarity in the thin air and the vast horizons—this was a thing the village could accept, perhaps even admire.

Luca rehearsed the narrative as he walked, testing it mentally for weakness. He had made a vow to pray in the heights, he would say. He had been called to seek spiritual grounding, and the Pollino peaks were the place where such seeking made sense. He could speak of it with the kind of quiet conviction that would make it credible, the kind of sincerity that the village respected. They were religious people by training and tradition, and they understood the pull of sacred space.

By the time he reached the edge of the tree line where the mountain began to transition into the more traveled roads, Luca had internalized the narrative so thoroughly that it felt almost true. He had begun to believe in the prayer narrative himself, or at least in believing in his ability to make others believe it. The mountain had called him—that was simple fact. That he was searching for Italus rather than enlightenment was a detail that did not need to change the basic shape of his explanation.

The path narrowed as it descended further, becoming the familiar trail that led toward the lower slopes where the paths were more regularly traveled. Luca moved through this transition point with the comfortable certainty of repeated passage, his body knowing the terrain without his mind needing to direct each step.

It was here, where the higher country opened into the lower valleys and the isolation of the peaks gave way to the possibility of encounter, that he became aware of being watched.

The sensation arrived first as a prickling at the back of his neck, the kind of physical awareness that spoke of another presence even before conscious observation could identify it. Luca did not break his stride, but his attention shifted, his senses expanding outward. The afternoon light was slanting through the trees at a lower angle now, and the shadows were growing longer. There were places for someone to conceal themselves in the growth along the path, and there were paths that led downslope from the ridge that would allow someone to intersect his descent without obviously appearing to do so.

Someone had been watching his repeated visits. That much he had suspected, had perhaps even known without consciously acknowledging the knowledge. The feeling of observation had grown stronger with each trip, as though attention itself were a physical pressure that accumulated over time. Now that presence had manifested into something closer to direct encounter.

Luca continued walking, his pace unchanged, his expression neutral. Whoever was watching would reveal themselves if the watching was meant to lead to confrontation. If it was merely observation, then showing that he had noticed would accomplish nothing except to alert them to his awareness. Better to continue as though unaware, to allow the encounter to unfold according to its own logic.

The figure emerged from the tree line perhaps fifty strides ahead, moving to intercept the path with the kind of deliberate purpose that suggested calculation and planning. As the distance closed, Luca could make out details: a man of middle years, dressed in the dark robes of a mountain monk or hermit, his face weathered and marked with the kind of premature aging that the high country imposed on those who chose to live in its isolation.

The monk raised a hand in greeting, not hostile but authoritative, as though he had every right to stand in the center of the path and demand Luca's attention.

Luca slowed his pace and came to a stop a few strides away from the man, close enough for conversation, far enough for safety should safety become a matter of concern.

"You make the climb often," the monk said. His voice carried the rough textures of someone whose normal life did not include much speech. The words came measured and careful, as though he was taking time to consider each one before releasing it.

"I do," Luca said. He had decided already that he would not lie to this man unless pressed to do so. Something in the monk's bearing suggested that lying would be recognized and rejected, and that the monk had earned enough authority through his obvious knowledge of Luca's patterns that dismissal would not be wise.

"Your excuses grow thin," the monk said. "Your family begins to notice, and when families notice, communities follow. Soon there will be talk about why a boy of your age finds need to climb so frequently to pray alone. Not all talk will be kind."

Luca felt something shift in his chest, a mixture of fear and recognition. This man had been watching long enough to know his circumstances, his family situation, his social position in the village. The knowledge itself was a kind of violation, but it was also a kind of care, a kind of attention that suggested the watching was not casual.

"I don't know what you want from me," Luca said carefully.

"I want you to have a credible story to tell," the monk said. "Prayer is good. Prayer is acceptable. Prayer is the kind of thing that families understand and communities approve. You will tell them that you have made a vow to pray in the high places, and that you have committed yourself to a discipline of spiritual seeking. You will speak of it with the kind of quiet conviction that makes truth, whether it is truth or not."

Something in the monk's phrasing suggested that truth and conviction were not necessarily the same thing, that the act of speaking with conviction could transform a thing into truth through the sheer force of belief and social acceptance.

"Why should I listen to you?" Luca asked.

"Because you are doing something that will bring danger to yourself and those around you if you do not establish a better cover," the monk said. "Because your excuses are failing, and you will be followed or watched or prevented from returning to these heights if you do not learn to move through your life more carefully. Because I am offering you a tool that will allow you to continue what you are doing without bringing suspicion and consequence down on your family."

Luca studied the monk's face, trying to read intention in the weathered lines and the dark eyes that had seen many years and many things. There was something familiar in those eyes, something that resonated with the memory of the storm, though Luca could not have named what or how.

"Who are you?" Luca asked.

"I am a monk," the man said. "I live in these heights, seeking solitude and the presence of God. I am a person who notices things, and I have noticed you."

That was not an answer to the question Luca had asked, but it was the only answer the monk seemed willing to give. Luca could push for more information, could insist on identification and explanation. But something in the monk's bearing suggested that pushing would yield nothing except the reinforcement of the boundaries the monk had already established.

"If I tell them I am praying," Luca said slowly, "it will be true. At least in part. I came to this place seeking something, and I did not know what to call it. Perhaps it is prayer. Perhaps it is seeking. The names matter less than the reality."

The monk nodded as though Luca had arrived at something important, something that vindicated the entire conversation.

"Then your story is true enough," the monk said. "Tell them this, and continue your seeking. Continue coming to these heights. But do it with the blessing of a spiritual practice, not the suspicion of a boy with hidden purposes."

"And you?" Luca asked. "What will you do?"

The monk turned slightly, as though preparing to leave, to disappear back into the trees from which he had emerged.

"I will watch," he said. "I will keep knowledge of what you are doing. When you need guidance, you may find me, though you may not always recognize the form that guidance takes. And you will learn to move through the world more carefully, with more consciousness of the impact your actions create on those around you."

The monk began to walk past him, and Luca felt the impulse to turn and follow, to continue the conversation, to extract more information. He restrained the impulse, holding himself still and allowing the monk to pass. By the time curiosity overcame caution and Luca turned to look back, the man had already disappeared into the afternoon shadows of the lower slopes, moving with the kind of efficiency that suggested he knew these paths far better than any casual wanderer would know them.

Luca stood alone on the trail, the weight of the conversation settling around him like something physical. The monk had offered him a gift—the gift of a credible story, the gift of permission to continue his seeking without social consequence. In return, the monk had established himself as a presence in Luca's life, as an observer and a guide who would shape his movement through the world going forward.

Luca began walking again, descending toward the village and the family and the life that waited for him in the lower elevations. The sun was now low enough that he would arrive home only slightly after the time when work should be concluding, when his mother would be preparing the evening meal and his father would be tending to the livestock in the fading light.

He would tell them about his vow to pray. He would speak with the quiet conviction that transformed narrative into truth through repetition and social acceptance. He would build a fortress of piety around his repeated absences, and none of them would question it because people did not question the spiritual seeking of the young. It was an acceptable mystery, unlike the mystery of why he kept returning to the high places. Prayer was a thing one did not fully explain, a thing one lived and embodied rather than defended with words.

The first practical concealment habit had begun to form in Luca's mind as a structure, as a discipline. The prayer narrative would need to be maintained consistently, amplified through his actions and his demeanor, reinforced through small gestures and choices that demonstrated his spiritual commitment. He would need to develop genuine patterns of piety that would support the story, or at least patterns that were consistent enough that they would not invite further inquiry.

And somewhere above him, somewhere in the high places where the storm had changed Italus and Farovald and left its mark on the terrain, his strange creature moved through the landscape, leaving traces that only Luca had been called to read. The monk had known about the climbing, had watched long enough to measure the frequency and commitment. But the monk had not mentioned Italus. The monk had offered guidance about how to continue seeking without social consequence, but had not acknowledged what was being sought.

This too was meaningful. This too was information encoded in silence and careful omission.

By the time Luca reached the outskirts of the village, the sun had touched the horizon and the long summer light was beginning its slow transition toward dusk. The rhythm of communal life was changing—work shifting toward rest, activity toward gathering, the dispersed functions of the day consolidating into the shared spaces where families came together. He moved toward his home with the step of someone who had been on a spiritual retreat, whose body was tired from walking and whose mind was elevated by contemplation and prayer.

The prayer narrative was already becoming true through the simple act of embodying it. By the time he reached his family's threshold, Luca had begun to believe in the story he was constructing, had begun to feel the weight of a vow that he had not actually made but had committed himself to maintaining.

His mother was waiting at the door when he arrived, her expression a mixture of relief and concern. She did not ask him where he had been. Instead, she reached out and steadied him with a hand on his arm, as though she could feel through the physical contact that he had been somewhere difficult, somewhere that required endurance and commitment.

"You are safe," she said. It was not a question.

"I am safe," Luca confirmed. "I have found what I needed to find."

He did not tell her that what he needed to find was moving. He did not tell her that a creature with an impossible name inhabited the high places and had drawn him back to the Pollino peaks over and over again. He did not tell her that an old monk with weathered hands and knowing eyes had intercepted him on the trail and offered guidance that amounted to permission.

Instead, he let her lead him into the house, where the smell of cooking filled the air and his sister was setting the table for the evening meal. He sat with them as they ate, and he spoke about the beauty of the high country and the clarity that came from time spent in solitude. He spoke about prayer, and about spiritual seeking, and about the way that mountains offered a connection to something larger than oneself.

Every word was true, and none of it was what was actually occurring. The combination was seamless and complete, the perfect camouflage of truth layered over secret.

# Chapter One

The roar filled the whole sky. Not sound exactly, but a presence that stripped away everything else. Two figures stood in the mountain pass, exposed on high ground as the storm descended across the Pollino ridge. The older man, his hair dark and wild, had already been altered. His hands bore the white scars of an earlier lightning strike, palms marked like stigmata from something he had touched or been touched by years before. The younger one beside him, still new to whatever power ran through them both, felt the electricity gathering in the air like a held breath. The mountain itself seemed to wait. Then the lightning came not as separate bolts but as a unified force, a current that moved through both men simultaneously, binding them in the same white instant. When it passed, they remained standing. Changed. Neither spoke of it afterward, but the memory lived in their bodies, in the cellular knowledge that something fundamental had shifted in that moment when the storm made them singular.

The memory dissolved like mist burning away at dawn.

Luca crouched in the morning quiet of the Pollino heights, the air already warming, and forced his attention back to the ground beneath his hands. The storm memory faded as his fingers traced the scored earth. Someone had moved recently through this pass. The ground bore fresh marks, deliberate disturbances where something heavy had been dragged or carried across stones that should have remained undisturbed through seasons of wind and rain and frost.

He pressed his palm against the earth, feeling for warmth that might suggest recent passage. Nothing. The disturbance was old enough to have lost the body heat of whoever had caused it, but fresh enough that no morning rain had yet settled the displaced soil back into its proper alignment. Three days, perhaps four. The calculation came to him with the ease of long practice. He had been coming to this place every day for weeks now, mapping its small changes, learning its rhythms. The routine had become so familiar that the breaks in it stood out like scars on skin.

The pine tree should have been here. That was the real evidence, the disruption that had pulled him up the mountain again this morning despite his mother's questions about his errands and the village priest's gentle inquiries about his frequent wandering. There had been a particular tree marking this point in the landscape, a gnarled pine with a trunk thick enough that two men would need to stretch their arms around it to clasp hands. Luca had noted its position weeks ago, had used it as a fixed point for his internal surveying. Now the space where it should have stood held only open air. Not fallen—he had found no remnants, no needles scattered, no broken branches suggesting wind damage. Moved. The tree had been deliberately uprooted or cut down and removed from this location.

He stood and turned slowly, trying to reconstruct the landscape as it should have been. The rock formations to the west remained unchanged. The small spring that ran only in late winter still marked the eastern boundary of this clearing. But the tree's absence created a gap in his mental map, a blank space where there should have been orientation. His eyes felt the dislocation. When he tried to pace out the distance from this point to the next landmark, his counting seemed wrong. The space stretched longer than it should have been. Or perhaps contracted. The disorientation came in waves, a dizziness that had nothing to do with the altitude and everything to do with standing in a place that had been deliberately altered to confuse precise reckoning.

This was what Luca had begun to understand over the past month. Someone was hiding here. Someone was using this mountain as shelter, and that someone knew enough to understand that the small markers of the landscape could tell a story to anyone paying close attention. The missing tree was not an accident of nature. It was a deliberate obstruction of someone else's ability to track movement through this terrain.

The marks on the ground pointed generally northward, toward the steeper reaches of the Pollino where the rock faces rose too high for comfortable climbing. Luca had not followed in that direction yet. The ground there was different, unforgiving. He would need better light and more time, and more convincing lies to tell when he returned to the village. Already, the excuses were becoming thin. His mother had begun to watch him with a careful attention that suggested she knew he was not simply gathering herbs or hunting game. The priest had stopped asking questions directly and had instead begun mentioning prayer, suggesting that if Luca found comfort in solitude on the heights, perhaps he might bring devotional intent to his wanderings rather than leaving them as purpose-less rambling.

Luca settled into a crouch and studied the ground more carefully, running his fingers along the scored earth. The pattern suggested something substantial had been moved. An animal, perhaps. But the marks were too regular, too deliberately arranged. A person dragging supplies. A person establishing a camp and then moving everything to avoid discovery. A person who understood that the wilderness could be read by anyone who knew the language of leaves and earth and stone.

He had come to suspect that the person he was tracking might be the creature his village spoke of in low voices. Italus. The impossible thing that old Vittoria claimed to have seen, the beast that left no clear prints but moved through the mountains like a shadow with agency. Most of the village dismissed her account. She was ancient and prone to visions. But Luca had grown up listening to the particular quality of her voice when she spoke of what she had seen. There was no tremor of fabrication in it, no embellishment. She had encountered something real, something that did not move like the wolves or the wild boars that occasionally came down from the high passes.

The thought should have frightened him. Instead, it drew him back up the mountain every day despite the growing suspicion in his mother's eyes and the priest's gentle suggestions of more appropriate devotions.

He rose and moved deeper into the clearing, walking the perimeter slowly, looking for signs he might have missed on earlier visits. Disturbed moss on a rock face. Scratches on stone that might indicate handholds. A place where the soil had been deliberately tamped down in a pattern that suggested repeated use. The work required patience and the kind of detailed attention that most people never learned to apply to the landscape. Luca had learned it from necessity, from years of needing to know exactly where water would run during storms and which paths would be safe when snow came to the high places. The skill that the village assumed was simple hillside gathering had become something more precise, more purposeful.

A sound from above made him still. Not a large sound. Not immediately alarming. Just the smallest disruption of the quiet, the kind of noise that a person makes when they try to move silently and forget that their own breathing can give away their presence. Luca turned slowly, his hand moving to the knife at his belt, but he saw nothing in the rocks above him. Whoever or whatever had made the sound had either moved out of sight or been only the wind, an animal, the mountain itself settling into the morning.

He forced himself to wait for a full minute before resuming his search, using the time to control his heart rate, to push down the sudden alertness that the sound had triggered. If something was watching from the rocks above, it would not help to show fear. Predators responded to fear. Luca had learned that too, from the stories of hunters and from watching the way the village dogs reacted when wild things came close to human habitation.

By midday, his legs ached and his throat was dry. He had found three more sites of disturbance, all pointing in roughly the same direction, all suggesting a pattern of regular passage through this particular route. He had not discovered an actual camp, no evidence of a shelter or a fire. But the trail was clear enough to someone who knew how to read it. Whatever was moving through these mountains was intelligent. It was careful. It was not simply wandering but traveling with purpose, using knowledge of the landscape that suggested either long familiarity or something more fundamental, an instinctive understanding of how to move through stone and earth and shadow.

The vertigo came again as he tried to stand. His legs were steady enough, but his mind seemed to slip sideways, losing its grip on the spatial relationships that should have been simple and obvious. The missing tree. The altered ground. The paths that twisted in ways that felt almost deliberate in their disruption of expected patterns. Luca closed his eyes and forced himself to breathe, to wait for his sense of orientation to settle. When he opened them again, the dizziness had passed, but something in the air felt different. The quality of the light had changed, or the temperature, or some essential property of the moment that he could not quite name.

He turned to head back down the mountain, moving more quickly than was strictly safe on the uneven ground. The village would be expecting him by evening. He had told his mother he was hunting. It was his standard excuse, and it had begun to wear thin. Soon he would need new reasons for his absences, or he would need to give up these daily expeditions and accept that he would never know whether Vittoria's claim was true, whether something genuinely moved through the Pollino heights, whether the altered landscape was trying to tell him something urgent that he was too young or too uninformed to quite understand.

The path down took him through a narrow passage between rock faces, a place where the light seemed to fall at an odd angle and where the air held a perpetual coolness even in the warmth of the summer day. This was where he encountered the man.

The figure stood in the passage ahead, blocking the path forward. He was tall and lean, dressed in the rough cloth and poor sandals of a hermit or a monk, his face weathered dark by years of sun and wind. He held no weapon, made no threatening gesture, but his presence in the passage was clearly deliberate. He had not simply happened to be here. He had been waiting, or hunting, or performing some kind of observation that had positioned him exactly where Luca would have to pass.

Luca stopped, his hand tightening on the knife hilt. The man did not move, and for a moment, neither did the boy. The silence stretched between them, filled with the soft sound of wind through the rock passage and the distant call of something bird-like from higher up the mountain.

"You come here often," the man said. His voice was rough, as if he had not used it in a long time. His hands, which hung loose at his sides, were marked with old scars that ran from his palms up toward his wrists. The scarring was unlike anything Luca had ever seen, a pattern that looked almost deliberate, almost like someone had pressed themselves against something very hot and held there long enough to mark every line of skin. "Every day, perhaps. Or nearly every day. Your pattern is becoming obvious to anyone who watches the mountain carefully."

Luca did not answer immediately. He was assessing the man, trying to determine whether he represented danger and whether running was a viable option. The passage was narrow. If he ran, the man could pursue more easily than if they fought. If he stood his ground, he might be able to make use of the knife if things came to violence. But the man's tone had not been threatening, merely observational. He seemed more interested in establishing that he had noticed something than in using that notice for aggression.

"The herbs are good in this place," Luca said finally. "My mother has use for them. I gather what I can."

The man's expression did not change. He looked down at Luca's hands, which held no gathered plants, carried no basket or cloth for collecting anything. "You gather herbs," he repeated, and there was something in his voice that suggested he found the claim amusing or perhaps merely sad. "You gather herbs by moving in a pattern that mimics tracking. By studying the ground like someone learning to read a language. By searching for something that cannot be easily found, that does not want to be easily found."

Luca felt heat rise into his face. He was caught, and the man knew it. There was no point in continuing the pretense.

"There is something here," Luca said. "In these mountains. I want to know what it is."

The man was quiet for a long moment. He lifted one scarred hand and studied it, turning it palm-down as if he had never quite looked at it properly before. "Your curiosity will bring you into danger," he said. "Not immediately, perhaps. But in time. There are things in these mountains that are not meant to be found, not by the young and not by the unprepared. Your mother would do better to have you marry young, settle yourself in the village, learn the business of growing things in soil that does not move beneath you. This place, these heights, this pursuit of mysteries that do not welcome investigation. These things will change you in ways that cannot be undone."

"Are you the thing that lives here?" Luca asked. He did not know where the boldness came from, but now that the words were spoken, he found he did not regret them. "Are you what I have been tracking?"

"I am a monk," the man said. His voice had settled into something gentler. "I keep the prayers in this place because prayer is sometimes what a mountain needs. I am old, and I have learned that solitude is a kind of honesty. I do not explain myself to the village, and I do not invite the village to explain itself to me. I am content with that arrangement."

It was too pat an answer, too rehearsed. Luca could hear the lie in it the way he could read tracks, through small disruptions in the expected pattern. But he also understood that the man had given him what he was willing to give, and that pressing further would only result in silence.

"I will stop coming," Luca said. It was not true. He knew already that he would not stop, that the pull toward these mountains was too strong now, that something about the disturbances in the landscape had caught hold of him and would not release him easily. But he said the words anyway, as a kind of courtesy to the stranger who had been kind enough to intercept him in the passage rather than allowing him to stumble upon something he was not ready to know.

The man studied him for a long moment. When he spoke again, his voice carried something that might have been approval or might have been resignation. "You will come back," he said. "That much is obvious. But you are being observed now, which means your family is beginning to question your absences. You need a better reason for being here. A reason that they will accept without doubt, something that will satisfy even the village priest and his concerns about souls wandering away from proper devotion."

"What reason?" Luca asked.

"Prayer," the man said simply. "Tell your mother that you have begun to climb these heights to pray. Tell her that the priest's words have moved you to seek communion with God in the quiet places, away from the village distractions. Tell her that you come here to think of your soul and the state of your immortal nature. No village mother will question such devotion. No priest will do anything but encourage it. You will have your freedom to move through these mountains, and the village will sleep easy knowing that you are using your time for purposes they understand and approve."

It was remarkably practical advice, the kind of thing that showed real understanding of how the village functioned, how the people who lived there thought. Luca filed it away, already composing the words he would use the next time his mother asked where he had been.

"What is your name?" Luca asked.

"I am called Farovald," the man said. "I have been in these mountains for longer than you have been alive, and I expect I will remain here long after you have returned to the village and made your own peace with a simpler life. I am telling you this because you will encounter me again, and I do not wish there to be fear between us. I am not your enemy, boy. But I am also not your guide or your teacher. I am simply someone who has learned to exist in this place in ways that the village would not understand. Remember that distinction."

He stepped aside, creating a clear path down the mountain. Luca walked past him slowly, still uncertain about the man's true nature, still not entirely convinced by the monk's explanation. But he was grateful for the practical advice about prayer, and he was grateful for the courtesy of the passage that had been offered.

Behind him, as he walked, Luca could feel Farovald's presence, a weight of attention and assessment. He did not look back. The descent required all his focus, all his skill at moving safely through terrain that seemed to shift beneath his feet. By the time he reached the lower slopes, the afternoon was already beginning its turn toward evening, and the village lights were starting to show through the mist that gathered in the valleys.

When his mother asked where he had been, Luca told her about the prayer. He told her that he had felt called to seek solitude on the heights, that something about the priest's sermons had moved him to want a deeper communion with God. His mother's face changed as he spoke, softened by an emotion that looked like pride or perhaps relief. She did not question him further. She welcomed him back to the house and had his father prepare extra food for his supper, as if she were rewarding him for this sudden piety.

The priest, when Luca saw him next in the village square, received the news with visible satisfaction. He placed a hand on Luca's shoulder and spoke of the boy's improved spiritual understanding, of the grace that God sometimes showed to the young when they opened their hearts to authentic seeking. Several older women nodded in agreement, and Luca watched as the story of his devotion spread through the village, taking on details and embellishments that he had never provided. By evening, he had become the spiritual hope of his family line, the child who had been called to deeper faith in these dangerous times when the young so often strayed from proper devotion.

His freedom to move through the mountains was now secured by a reason that no one in the village would ever question.

That night, Luca lay in his sleeping place and thought about the man in the passage, about the scars on his hands, about the way he had seemed to know exactly what Luca was doing and why. He thought about the missing tree and the altered ground, about the trail that led northward toward the steeper reaches of the Pollino. He thought about the brief moment when the dizzy disorientation had come over him, when the landscape had seemed to slip sideways and reveal something beneath itself, something that ordinary sight could not quite perceive.

In the darkness, he made his first deliberate choice about what he would hide from his family, what he would not speak of, what he would keep as a private knowledge that belonged only to himself and to the mountains. It was a small beginning, hardly noticeable as a turning point in a life. But it was real, and it was his, and once made, it could not be unmade.

He would return to the Pollino tomorrow under the cover of prayer and spiritual seeking. He would continue to track the disturbances in the landscape. He would learn to move through this place without leaving marks of his own passage that others could read. And he would do all of this quietly, carefully, understanding now that he was no longer simply a curious village boy wandering in the mountains. He was beginning to be someone else, someone marked by the knowledge of something strange and significant that moved through the Pollino heights, something that had already, through the intervention of Farovald, begun to teach him the first small lessons of concealment and deliberate ignorance.

The lessons would grow more complex as time passed. The skills would deepen. The secrets would multiply like shadows gathering in the mountain passes. But for now, in this first night of his deliberate separation from the simple understanding of his childhood, Luca knew only that he had begun something that could not be stopped, and that he was grateful for the man who had given him permission to continue it without drawing the attention of those who loved him but could not possibly understand what he was trying to learn.
