# Chapter One

The roar of the storm consumed everything. Sky and earth had become one violent thing, and the air itself burned. Two figures stood at the mountain's crown, their bodies rigid against the deluge, and in the instant before the lightning struck, they saw each other with a clarity that no ordinary light could grant. The bolt came down through them both, and in that fraction of a second before their nerve systems began to scream, they understood something together, a shared knowing that would mark them both for the remainder of their separate lives. It was not revelation. It was alteration. The lightning did not burn away what they were; it changed the substance of what they would become. Their palms blistered. Their vision fractured into colors that no ordinary eye should perceive. The smell of scorched flesh and ozone fused into something else, something that would come back to them in dreams and in the sudden moments between waking and sleep. When the thunder finally ended and they collapsed into the driving rain, they were no longer quite themselves.

Two hundred years passed.

The quiet of the Pollino heights felt different now, thin and deliberate, as though the mountain itself were holding its breath. Luca knelt beside the scored earth, running his fingers across the exposed soil where something heavy and deliberate had torn through the forest floor. The ground was still fresh. Particles of dark loam clung to his fingernails, and the edges of the disturbance had not yet begun to crumble or weather. Whatever had moved through here had done so recently, within days perhaps, or even more recently than that.

His eyes traced a line deeper into the forest. The pines here grew with a particular geometry that Luca had come to know with an almost painful intimacy over the past months. He had spent so many afternoons pacing these slopes, measuring them against some internal map he had built through repetition and careful observation. Each tree held a place in his mental survey. Each rock formation, each stand of scrub, each visible patch of exposed limestone formed part of an architecture that existed now only in his memory.

But something had changed.

Luca straightened and moved forward, stepping carefully across the disturbed ground. To his left, where a particular pine should have stood, there was now nothing but empty space and a faint depression in the needle-thick soil. He could see the rough outline where the tree's base had rested, a circle of deeper discoloration perhaps six paces from where he now stood. The tree itself was gone. It had not fallen naturally; no splintered trunk lay among the undergrowth, no broken branches hung from surrounding growth. It had been moved. Deliberately. Methodically.

Luca's breath came harder now. This was not imagination or the trick of a half-remembered landscape. This was physical fact, as real and irrefutable as the earth itself. Someone had come here. Someone had taken the time and effort to uproot a mature tree and move it elsewhere. Italus. It had to be Italus.

For months now, Luca had pursued the shape of a pattern, following traces that seemed to shift and dissolve whenever he drew close. The hermit had left the settlement at Saracena almost seven years ago, had vanished into the high places without explanation or farewell. The people who had known him simply accepted his departure as the inevitable choice of a man too strange for ordinary community. But Luca remembered the shape of Italus's hands. He remembered the way the old man had watched the children play with an intensity that seemed to encompass more than mere observation. He remembered conversations, brief and strange, in which Italus had posed questions that seemed to circle around knowledge that he already possessed.

And then, almost a year ago, Luca had found evidence that Italus had returned to the Pollino. Not to the village. Not to any inhabited place. But to the heights. To this particular region of the mountain, which seemed to have drawn him with an insistence that suggested purpose rather than chance.

The evidence had been subtle at first. A cleared patch of undergrowth where a shelter had been constructed and then abandoned. A series of marks on the stones that might have been accidental or might have been intentional. But they had compelled Luca to return, again and again, to walk the same paths and cover the same ground, searching for confirmation of a presence that seemed to exist just beyond the edge of proof.

His family had begun to notice. His mother had asked why he spent so many afternoons on the heights when there was work to be done in the village. His sister had made comments about his distraction, about the way he seemed to listen for sounds that no one else could hear. The priest had suggested, with barely concealed skepticism, that Luca was developing the calling of a monk himself, so devoted was he to solitary wandering. Even his father had raised an eyebrow when Luca had returned with torn clothing and scraped hands, requiring explanations that grew progressively weaker and less credible with each successive visit.

Now, standing before the empty space where a tree should have been, Luca felt the weight of those increasing scrutinies. He knew that his excuses were wearing thin. He could not return to the village and speak the truth: that he was tracking a phantom, following the erratic trail of a man who might not exist in any present sense at all. How could he explain his compulsion to his family, to the village, to himself? What reason could he offer that would sound sane?

Yet here was the evidence, incontrovertible and physical. The tree had been moved. The ground had been disturbed. Something had changed in this landscape that Luca knew with intimate precision.

He began to pace out the area methodically, measuring it with the careful stride he had developed over months of surveying. The disturbance extended in a roughly westward direction, following the natural descent of the slope but deliberately chosen rather than accidental. Whoever had moved through here had known where they were going. They had selected a path that was concealed enough to avoid immediate notice but deliberate enough to suggest purpose.

As Luca traced the line of disturbance, a wave of vertigo suddenly seized him. The mountain seemed to shift beneath his feet, the orientation of stones and trees and sky fragmenting into components that no longer cohered into a single stable space. His mind, which had been so carefully constructing and maintaining its precise map of the landscape, suddenly faltered. The effort of holding all those measurements and spatial relationships in consciousness at once, while simultaneously registering the way that landscape had been altered, created a disorientation that felt almost physical. The ground seemed to tilt. The sky pressed down. For a moment, Luca could not remember which direction was upslope and which was down.

He sat down abruptly on a nearby stone, his breath coming in short gasps. The sensation slowly began to recede, replaced by a hollow exhaustion. He had pushed too hard into the work of observation. He had maintained the intensity of focus for too long. Or perhaps it was something else entirely, something that arose from the fundamental wrongness of finding that a landscape he thought he understood had been deliberately altered by forces outside his comprehension or control.

When the dizziness finally faded enough for him to trust his legs again, Luca gathered what he could see of the evidence. He did not take anything physical; he simply committed the details to memory with the same methodical intensity he brought to everything else. The angle of the tree's former base. The pattern of the scored earth. The direction of the disturbance leading deeper into the forest. All of it was stored now in the careful architecture of his mind, another piece of the puzzle that he was assembling without knowing what the final picture might resemble.

He would have to come back. He would have to construct some new excuse, some fresh explanation for his family and the village that might carry a little more weight than the previous ones. But he knew, with a certainty that felt like cold metal in his chest, that he would find a way. Because whatever Italus was doing here, whatever purpose had drawn him to the high places of the Pollino and compelled him to methodically alter the landscape itself, Luca needed to understand it.

He needed to know.

Over the following weeks, Luca's visits to the Pollino heights became more frequent and more desperate. He returned three times in the first ten days alone, each time pushing a little deeper into the forest, searching for signs that the disturbance had been followed by further movement or change. His family's patience began to visibly fray. His mother started asking sharper questions about where he spent his time. His sister made open comments about how thin he was becoming, how distracted he seemed at the evening meal. Even the younger children had begun to notice his peculiar intensity, and they had taken to mimicking his solitary wanderings with a mockery that stung precisely because they did not understand its target.

At the market, Luca overheard two women discussing his behavior. They had not meant him to hear them; they were speaking in low tones while he was selecting vegetables for his mother. But their voices carried enough to reach him, and the words lodged in his memory with painful clarity. Strange boy. Getting stranger. Probably ends up like Italus, they had said. Or worse. The priest should speak to his father.

Luca had selected his vegetables and left without looking at them again.

The practical difficulty of maintaining his search was becoming acute. He could not simply vanish for hours at a time without explanation. He could not emerge from the forest with torn clothing and scraped hands without having to account for the damage. More subtly, his own internal resources were beginning to flag. The intensity of focus that he had maintained for so long was starting to create a kind of fatigue that sleep did not seem to cure. His dreams were filled with images of altered landscape, trees that should be present but were not, ground that had been scored by forces he could not identify. He would wake in the darkness with his heart racing, convinced for a moment that he had missed some crucial detail, some piece of evidence that would unlock the entire mystery.

It was on an afternoon in the third week of his renewed searching that Luca encountered the monk.

He had taken the longer route up to the heights that day, deliberately avoiding the most direct paths in hope of finding fresh evidence approaching from a different angle. The afternoon was growing long, and he was moving quickly through terrain that he had not thoroughly surveyed before, when he became aware that he was no longer alone on the mountain.

At first, he thought it was merely the way the shadows fell between the trees, or the subtle movement of a larger animal in the undergrowth. But as he paused and listened, he became certain of a human presence. Someone was moving through the forest behind him, perhaps fifty paces back, matching his pace with a precision that suggested deliberate tracking rather than coincidence.

Luca's first impulse was to move faster, to break into a run and put distance between himself and whatever followed. But he forced himself to stop instead, turning to face back down the slope, waiting to see who would emerge.

The man who appeared from between the pines was dressed in a simple woolen habit, the rough cloth of a mountain monk. His age was difficult to determine; his face was weathered by sun and wind, and his hair had gone entirely gray. He carried nothing with him, no staff, no visible provisions, just the habit and a rope belt tied around his waist. But it was his hands that caught Luca's attention. They were marked with old scarring, pale marks that stood out against his weathered skin, patterns that looked almost like burn damage.

"You move through these heights with unusual frequency, boy," the monk said. His voice was rough, as though he did not use it often, but his Latin was clear. "And your excuses grow weaker with each visit."

Luca felt his face flush. "I have reasons," he said, trying to keep his voice steady. "My business on the mountain is my own."

"Of course it is," the monk agreed. "But you become less successful at keeping it secret with each visit to Saracena and back. The village notices things, even if they do not yet understand what they are noticing. And your family begins to speak about you in ways that suggest they are becoming alarmed."

Luca said nothing. He could not deny the truth of the monk's observation.

"You are searching for something," the man continued, moving a few paces closer but stopping at a respectful distance. "Or someone. And whatever you are searching for, you have decided that secrecy is necessary. That suggests either danger or shame. Possibly both."

"Why does it matter to you?" Luca asked, defensive now. "There are many monks in the Pollino. Why should you concern yourself with a boy from the village?"

The monk smiled, a thin expression that changed the lines of his weathered face. "Because I know this mountain, boy. I know its paths and its places. And I know when something moves through it with purpose. You move with purpose. And you are moving toward something that you do not fully understand."

Luca wanted to turn and walk away. But something in the monk's words held him. This man knew the mountain. This man moved through it with the ease of someone who had spent years learning its paths. This man, with his burnt and scarred hands, seemed to know far more than he should about Luca's private searches.

"You cannot continue as you are doing," the monk said. "Your excuses will fail you within days or weeks at most. Your family will forbid your return to the heights. Your secret will be forced into the open, and you will have achieved nothing but the loss of your freedom to search at all."

"Then what do you suggest?" Luca asked, hearing the desperation in his own voice. "I cannot stop. I cannot explain. And I cannot continue indefinitely without being stopped."

"There is another way," the monk said. "Prayer. Spiritual seeking. You are young, and the village understands when the young feel drawn to contemplate higher things. If you tell your family that you have felt a calling to the contemplative life, that you wish to spend time in prayer and meditation on the mountain, they will understand. It will satisfy their curiosity. It will provide you with credible reason to return to these heights as frequently as you wish. And no one will question the solitary habits of a boy seeking connection with God."

Luca stared at the monk, considering the suggestion. It was audacious, and it relied on a kind of dissimulation that he had not previously considered. Yet it was also practical. It would provide him with the cover he needed to continue his search. It would transform his repeated visits from a source of family anxiety into something that would meet with approval, or at least resigned acceptance.

"How do you know so much about my situation?" Luca asked.

"I know the mountain," the monk repeated. "And I have spent enough time in the vicinity of the village to understand its patterns and its concerns. You are not the first young person to wrestle with questions of calling and purpose. But you are unusually intense in your searching."

Over the following weeks, as Luca implemented the monk's suggestion and began to frame his repeated visits to the Pollino as spiritual seeking, he began also to develop more sophisticated techniques of concealment. He learned to move through the forest in ways that left less evidence of his passage. He started to time his visits so that they fell within windows when his family would not notice his absence. He developed small rituals of prayer and meditation that he could genuinely perform while on the mountain, so that if anyone ever happened to observe him, they would find exactly what his stated purposes suggested.

He did not see the monk again after that afternoon, but the man's presence seemed to linger in the efficiency that Luca brought to his new practices. It was as though the encounter had crystallized something that had been diffuse and struggling before. Luca was no longer simply a boy pursuing an incomprehensible compulsion. He was becoming someone who moved with purpose, who understood that secrecy required practice, who recognized that the most effective concealment was the one that worked because people believed in what they thought they were seeing.

And in the depths of the forest, in places where no one from the village was likely to wander, Luca continued his search for evidence of Italus. He did not find the hermit himself, not yet. But he found more signs. A shelter that had been occupied recently. A cache of provisions hidden beneath a natural overhang. Once, on a particularly fortunate afternoon, he found what appeared to be a sleeping place, marked by the depression of a body in dried leaves and the careful arrangement of stones that suggested intentional shelter-construction.

Italus was here. He was moving through the mountain with purpose and method. And Luca, through patience and the careful development of practical concealment, was beginning to understand the patterns of that movement.

The mountain itself seemed to hold its breath around him, waiting to see what he would do with this knowledge when he finally caught close enough to act upon it.

# Chapter One

The roar came first, a sound like the world tearing open. Rain hammered the pine's upper branches with such violence that each drop seemed to strike with purpose, as though the storm wanted something from the wood and resin. The air itself had turned electric, the space between earth and sky compressed into something unbearable. A man's hand gripped the trunk, palm flat against the bark, fingers splayed as though he could hold the tree steady against what was coming.

The lightning did not announce itself.

It simply arrived, a white fracture splitting the Pollino sky, and in that instant the man's palm burned. The resin beneath the bark ignited from within. The cambium layer, that vital ring where wood became wood, scorched and blackened. The tree's response was silent and complete: a searing through its living tissue, a violation written in char and rupture that would never fully heal. The man's hand convulsed, his body thrown backward by a force that had no mercy for flesh or intention. His palms blazed. His hair stood on end. The smell of his own burning reached him before the shock stole everything else.

Then darkness.

Then silence.

Then, slowly, the rain continued. It was only rain now. The electric charge had moved on. The man lay in the mountain mud, gasping, his hands scorched and trembling. The pine stood, its bark smoking faintly, its resin oozing from new wounds that exposed the pale wood beneath. Neither the man nor the tree understood what had just happened. Both would carry the memory of it for centuries.

The pain faded into numbness. The numbness into something else.

---

The roar of the storm abruptly dropped away.

Luca's eyes snapped open. For a moment he could not remember which sky he was under, whether the thunder was still coming, whether his own palms were burning. His heart hammered against his ribs as if trying to escape. He stood on the slope above the Pollino heights, and the afternoon was perfectly calm, perfectly ordinary, perfectly wrong.

The pine was not where it should be.

He had walked this path since he was small enough to sit in the back of his father's cart, herding their sheep through the high meadows when the grass was good. He knew every marker, every stone, every tree that stood in its appointed place like a sentinel. The massive Bosnian pine with its thick trunk and its distinctive scar of old bark that formed a shape almost like a face—that pine had stood here for longer than Luca had been alive. Longer than his father had been alive. It should be here.

It was not.

Luca began to pace. His boots crushed the dried grass. The earth beneath the tree's old position lay freshly disturbed, the soil scored and dark, roots torn upward and exposed to air that had never touched them. The root system sprawled outward like severed arteries, some still oozing a faint, pale fluid that smelled of resin. The disturbance was not old. Days, perhaps. A week at most. The uprooted ends of the roots were still lighter in color where the breaks were recent.

The tree itself was gone. Not cut down—Luca would have heard that, would have seen the stump. Not dead and collapsed where it stood. Simply gone. Moved. Displaced. The thought should have been impossible. Trees did not move. Trees did not walk across mountainsides like wounded animals seeking shelter.

Yet the evidence of its passage lay scattered across the slope. Where its roots had dragged through the soil, a faint trail showed itself to anyone looking closely. The grass was crushed. The stones had been displaced. Here and there, fragments of resin-stained bark clung to a jutting rock. Here, a patch of needles still green, torn from branches by the violence of whatever movement had transported this massive tree from its rooted place to somewhere else, somewhere further up the mountain, out of sight.

Luca's hands trembled. He pressed them against his thighs to still them. His mind raced through possibilities. A storm. A terrible storm could uproot a tree, could tear it from the earth and send it tumbling. But he had been here two days ago, and the tree had been standing. The weather yesterday had been mild. The air this morning had been clear. No storm had struck the Pollino since the spring.

Unless.

The memory of the dream came back to him. The terrible roar. The electric smell. The sensation of burning. He pushed it away. A dream. Only a dream. The mind playing tricks on a shepherd boy who spent too much time alone in the high places.

He forced himself to continue the survey. The point where the massive trunk had been anchored showed him the shape of the roots as they had torn free. The depression in the earth was still raw. Bits of fine soil still spilled downslope, loosened by whatever violence had extracted this tree from the ground. Luca knelt and ran his fingers across the torn wood where the roots had snapped. The breaks were fresh. No oxidation. No weathering. Days old at most.

When he stood, vertigo seized him. The slope seemed to tilt. The sky above the Pollino peaks swam in his vision like an inverted reflection in water. He had to sit down or fall down. He chose to sit. He chose to sit on the very spot where the tree should be rooted, where its vast weight should anchor itself against the mountain's press.

His family would want to know why he had come up here. The sheep were fine. He had checked them twice. His excuse wore thinner each time he used it, and he was using it more and more. The meadows are overgrazed. I need to scout the higher pastures. The wolves have been spotted further south. Lies, thin and transparent as silk. His father's eyes narrowed with each one. His mother asked fewer questions but watched him more carefully. His younger sister had already started whispering to the other children in the village. Something was wrong with Luca. He was strange. He was often gone.

He could not tell them the truth. He could not say the tree had moved. He could not say he had a dream of lightning and burning that felt more real than waking. He could not say that something in the Pollino landscape had changed, shifted, been violated in a way that made his skin prickle with a sense of deep wrongness.

The trail of the tree's passage was evident to him as he traced it further up the slope. It was a deliberate path, or as deliberate as such a thing could be. The heaviest disturbance lay along a line that climbed toward the high meadows and the ridge beyond. The grass was flattened. More bark clung to rocks along the way. A branch, still bearing needles, lay across a stone like a marker.

Luca followed it.

He did not know how long he had been walking when the man appeared. The figure emerged from the shadow of a cluster of rocks as though he had been waiting, as though he had expected Luca to come this way. He was tall and thin, with skin weathered by years of exposure. His robes were dark, the fabric frayed at the edges, the color of earth and ash. A monk. A hermit of the sort that Luca had heard about from the village women, men who retreated into the mountains to pray and fast and speak to God without the interference of churches or priests.

Farovald.

That was not how Luca thought of him at first. At first he was simply an old man with sharp eyes and hands that bore strange marks. The palms were scarred, the skin there tight and glossy, marked with pale lines that resembled burns. When he moved, he favored his right hand slightly, as though the muscles and tendons had been damaged and never fully healed.

"You come to this place often," the man said. His voice was rough, as though he did not use it much, as though speaking required an effort he had long since abandoned.

Luca froze. His heart, which had only just returned to a normal rhythm, began to race again. The old man stood between him and the direct route back down the slope. There was no threat in his posture, nothing overtly dangerous. Yet the feeling of exposure was immediate and complete. The man had seen him. The man had been watching.

"I tend the sheep," Luca said. The lie came out automatically. He had been using it for so long that it emerged without thought.

"You tend the sheep." The man nodded slowly. His eyes were pale, a faded blue like water in winter. "But you have not brought the sheep to this height in three weeks. I have been here. I have watched."

Luca said nothing. His mind scrambled for another excuse, another fabrication. The man seemed amused by this. A thin smile crossed his face.

"Your excuses are poor." He extended his hand slightly, as though inviting Luca to examine the scarred palms. "I come to this mountain to pray and to be away from the noise of the world. I have learned to see small things. Changes. Disruptions. The disturbance you have been investigating, the trail of something massive that has moved through this landscape—these are not natural events, boy. Something has happened here. Something that matters."

Luca wanted to speak. He wanted to deny, to offer another excuse, to turn and run back down the slope. Instead, he found himself unable to move. The monk's steady gaze held him in place.

"You cannot visit this place often without drawing attention," the man continued. "Your family has already begun to notice. The village speaks. You have the face of a shepherd who is not where his work requires him. It is only a matter of time before someone demands an explanation you cannot give."

"I can make an excuse," Luca whispered.

"You have already tried." The monk gestured at him with one scarred hand. "Your excuses fail because they are not plausible. Sheep do not require this much tending. Wolves do not strike without bodies or blood as evidence. The meadows do not change so much that you must scout them daily."

The old man turned and looked back at the trail Luca had been following. His expression grew distant, as though he were remembering something. When he spoke again, his voice had changed, had become almost gentle.

"Prayer," he said, "is a credible reason. A boy might come to the mountain to pray. To seek solitude. To speak to God away from the distractions of family and village. No one questions prayer. The Church supports it. Your parents might even be proud."

Luca understood what the man was offering. A cover. An excuse that would hold, that would satisfy the questions already forming in his family's eyes. His father would not approve, but he would not forbid it. His mother might even encourage it. Prayer was respectable. Prayer was safe.

"I do not know how to pray," Luca heard himself say.

The monk smiled again, and this time there was something almost kind in the expression. "Neither did I, once. It is easily learned. I can teach you, if you wish. I come to this mountain daily. You are welcome to join me."

It was not an offer Luca had expected. It was not a threat or an interrogation. It was simply an opportunity dressed up as kindness. A way forward. A path through the difficulty that was closing around him like the coils of a serpent. He thought of his sister's whispers. He thought of his father's narrowing eyes. He thought of the tree that had moved, the evidence of something impossible that he could not explain and could not ignore.

"Yes," Luca said. "Yes, I think I would like that."

The monk nodded as though this had been decided long before this moment, as though the outcome had been certain from the beginning. He turned and began walking back down the slope, moving slowly enough that Luca could follow. Neither of them spoke. The afternoon light slanted across the Pollino peaks, turning the stone golden.

Luca walked behind the strange old man, the scarred palms, the burning eyes that seemed to see everything. He did not know what he had just agreed to. He did not know that the thin excuse of prayer would become his anchor, his justification, his salvation. He did not know that the monk would become a fixture of his world, present but distant, watching from the margins.

He only knew that something had moved in the mountain. Something had changed. And the old man with the burned hands seemed to understand exactly what that meant.

Over the following days, Luca established a pattern. He would announce that he was going to the high meadows to pray. His parents exchanged a glance but did not forbid it. His father seemed almost relieved, as though this explained Luca's strange behavior in a way that made sense. A boy approaching manhood sometimes felt the need to speak to God. It was natural. It was normal.

Luca climbed the slopes regularly now, moving with purpose rather than desperate searching. He began to learn the prayer words that the monk taught him. They were strange words, Latin words that he did not fully understand but that had a rhythm, a pattern that his memory could hold. He learned to kneel on the hard stone. He learned to close his eyes and move his lips in silence.

But he was not praying.

In the moments when the monk was occupied with his own devotions, Luca continued to follow the trail. He found where Italus had come to rest, nearly a mile upslope from its original position. The massive tree lay half-sheltered in a rocky depression, its roots exposed to the air, its bark still bearing the marks of its violent displacement. Here the evidence of the tree's passage was complete. Here was where something had violently altered the landscape of the Pollino.

Luca began to understand that this was a secret. Not the monk's secret, but his own. The man with the burned palms had given him a tool, a way to return again and again to this place without raising suspicion. In return, Luca kept silent about what he found. He did not speak of the tree. He did not ask questions about the scarred hands or the old man's inexplicable knowledge of the disturbance.

And the monk, for his part, seemed content to simply watch. To observe. To be present in the way that a guardian might be present, close enough to intervene if necessary, but not interfering. Not yet.

Luca was beginning his first practical concealment habits, learning to walk a line between the world above and the world below. Learning to maintain two versions of himself. Learning that some knowledge must be kept close, protected, hidden from the people who loved him.

He did not know that he was being guarded. He only knew that the mountain had changed him, had drawn something out of him that could not go back.

And the monk, with his burned palms and his ancient eyes, watched and waited.

# Chapter One

The wind in the high Pollino carried the taste of resin and stone. It was late summer in the year 789, and the afternoon had begun to close itself off with the particular heaviness that came before storm. The air felt thick, almost conscious, the way it did when the mountains were preparing to move something through themselves.

But that was not the storm that mattered now.

Two hundred years earlier, in the same landscape, the lightning had come without warning. It arrived as a sound first—a crack that split the atmosphere into before and after—and then as a presence so absolute that it consumed thought. The figure who stood with one palm pressed against the rough bark of the mature pine tree had no time to pull away. The current ran through trunk and root, through cambium and resin, through the living wood and into the living hand that held it. The pine's skin blackened. The man's palm charred. For a single moment they were one burning thing.

Then the current passed, and they were separate again.

The smell of scorched flesh and volatilized resin hung in the aftermath. The storm moved away toward the coast, taking the sound of its own fury with it. The burned hand trembled. The burned tree stood rigid, its top limbs still smoking slightly, its east-facing bark split where the lightning's heat had forced the living water inside it to turn to steam. Deep in the cambium, thin lines of char traced the path the current had taken on its way down toward the roots. The resin would seep from these wounds for years. The tree would survive. The man would carry the mark on his palms for the rest of his life.

Neither of them knew yet what this moment would mean.

The roar of the storm abruptly dropped away. There was no transition, no gradual fading into quieter weather. One moment was the violence of the sky; the next moment was silence and the ordinary light of a summer afternoon in the high mountains. The sensory shock of it was almost physical, like falling suddenly into still water.

Luca blinked. His eyes refocused on the Pollino landscape spread before him, on the real terrain of 789, on the scored earth beneath his feet.

He was fourteen years old, and he was alone on the heights with a problem that made no logical sense.

The pine that should have been here was not where it should be. Luca had been coming to this particular stretch of high ground since he was old enough to bring the sheep this far up the mountain without his father's direct supervision. That had been two years ago, when the village's flocks needed the late-summer forage and someone had to stay with them in the thin grass that grew between the rock faces. In two years, he had walked every route twice, three times, four times. He knew the terrain the way he knew the contours of his own hands. He knew where the good water ran. He knew which stones had moss on the north side. He knew the old pine—the one that rose above the other growth, the one with the twisted upper branches and the massive trunk—the way a shepherd knew his favorite ram by the shape of its horn.

It had been here, in this place, for as long as he could remember. Certainly for his entire lifetime. Certainly for his father's lifetime. His father had mentioned it once, years ago, as a landmark for directing the movements of the herd. "If you get confused, look for the tall pine. If you can see it, you know you're not too high up or too far to the west."

Now it was gone.

Not dead. Not fallen. Not even obviously missing in a way Luca could point to and say, "Here, the tree was chopped down." Instead, the earth itself was wrong. There was disturbed ground in a rough ellipse around the place where the massive trunk should have been rooted. The soil was scored and turned over. Long pale roots hung exposed in the air, some of them thick as Luca's forearm, others thin as his fingers. The disruption looked fresh. Rain would have started to settle this earth, grass would have begun to cover it, if it had been exposed for more than a few days. But it looked almost raw.

Luca paced out the physical measurements of the disturbance, moving in careful squares, trying to read the pattern left in the ground. His mental mapping of the landscape wanted to find a coherent explanation. His eyes wanted to resolve the displaced earth into a simple story: a tree that had fallen, that had been uprooted in a storm, that the villagers had somehow carried off for wood. But the roots were still partially attached to some kind of organic matter deeper in the soil. And the pattern of the disturbance suggested not a fall but a deliberate movement, a shifting of weight from one place to another.

It was as though something very heavy had hauled itself out of the earth and then, at some point, replaced itself a dozen paces to the north.

The overwhelming mental effort of trying to read an altered, deceptive landscape triggered a wave of vertigo and spatial disorientation. Luca closed his eyes for a moment, grounding himself in the physical sensation of solid earth beneath his boots, the weight of his own body, the ordinary fact of his own breathing. When he opened his eyes again, the landscape had not rearranged itself. The disturbed earth was still there. The pine was still absent from the place where it should have been.

There were two possibilities. One was that he had misremembered the location of the tree. That his mind, working from two years of afternoon visits to high pasture, had somehow constructed a false memory of its position. Luca turned slowly, scanning the visible terrain. To the north and west, the ground dropped away toward a ravine. To the south and east, the slope was gentler, scattered with lower growth and exposed stone. Behind him, the peak of the mountain rose in a series of natural steps toward the thin air at the top. Ahead of him, the same gentle descent continued down toward the village lands.

He knew this place. He had stood in this exact spot at least a dozen times. The pine had been here, solid and real, rising up like a marker in the emptiness. He would not have invented a tree for his own mental map. That was not how his mind worked. His mind worked in measurements and correspondences. His mind took the landscape and reduced it to a series of coordinates. The tree had been here, had been useful to him, had been real.

Which meant the tree had moved.

Luca crouched beside the disturbed earth and examined the exposed roots more carefully. The soil that clung to them was damp deep down, suggesting that the disturbance was not ancient. The cut edges where roots had snapped or torn were still moist, not dried and darkened. Some of the smaller root filaments still had a faint greenish tinge. And there, on several of the larger roots, were scorches. Dark marks as though something very hot had burned across them, or as though they had been exposed to an intense flame.

He touched one of the marked roots carefully. The char was dry, established, not fresh from today. But it was not years old either. Months, perhaps. Or weeks.

Luca stood up and turned to look at the ground again, at the pattern of the disturbance, at the track it seemed to leave as it moved away to the north. His eyes followed it, and then his feet followed his eyes, moving from the central point of the displacement toward the sparse trees and rocky outcrops that marked the slopes in that direction.

The trail, if it was a trail, led him up and away from the main heights, toward a narrower section of the Pollino plateau where the earth began its final descent into the forests that covered the lower slopes. The going was rough here. Stones turned under his feet. The sparse grass gave way to exposed bedrock in places. And then, roughly a hundred paces from the place where the pine should have been, Luca saw it.

The tree was still upright. Its massive trunk rose from the earth, its twisted upper branches spreading out against the afternoon sky. But it was not in the place where Luca's mind had stored its location. It was here, in this new place, its position changed, its relationship to the landscape rearranged. And as Luca moved closer, he could see that the eastern face of the trunk was darker than the western face. The bark was charred in places. There were long black lines running up the wood, paths traced by something that had run through the living tree with intense heat.

Lightning. The marks looked like lightning damage.

But there had been no storm in the Pollino for weeks. The last substantial rain had fallen in early summer. The current weather had been dry, hot, without the kind of electrical tension in the air that preceded a good thunderstorm. And besides, if lightning had struck the tree here, in this location, why had it moved? Why was the earth around it so freshly disturbed?

Luca reached out and placed his palm against the scarred bark. The tree was alive. He could feel that in the subtle vibration that ran through the wood, the tiny pulsing of sap in the cambium beneath the burned surface. The lightning had not killed it. But it had marked it. It had changed it in some fundamental way that Luca could not articulate, some way that made him think of his father's stories about the old shepherds who had been struck by lightning in the high places and had come down from the mountains changed, seeing things that were not there, or refusing to see things that were.

The sun was beginning to move toward the western edge of the sky. Luca would need to return to the village soon. The sheep would need to be brought down from the heights before dark. His family would need to know where he had been. He had already had to make excuses twice in the past week for being on the heights longer than the herding duties strictly required. He had told his father that the grass was particularly good on the upper slopes this year, that the sheep would not thrive if he did not keep them there until the very end of the season. He had told his mother that he was searching for a missing lamb, the little one that had been born late and was still learning the boundaries of the flock.

Both of these stories were partially true. The grass was good. There was a missing lamb, though Luca privately suspected that a wolf or a lynx had taken it. But the real reason he kept returning to the heights was this. This mystery. This changed landscape. This tree that had moved or been moved, this earth that had been disturbed and then somehow resettled, this evidence of something that did not follow the ordinary rules of how things were supposed to happen.

He could not tell anyone. The village would have an explanation, a simple one that involved either the mundane or the supernatural. Either the tree had fallen in a storm that he had somehow not noticed, which would make him careless and unsuitable for the serious work of herding. Or the tree had been moved by something that lived in the mountains, something that took what it wanted and rearranged the landscape according to its own purposes, which would make him dangerous to bring back into the village at all. Better to say nothing. Better to come back as often as he could manage with whatever excuses he could construct. Better to understand this alone.

Luca turned away from the scarred pine and began to make his way back down the slope, back toward where the main flock would be waiting for him to bring them together for the evening descent. The path down was steep in places, loose rock underfoot. He moved carefully, his mind still occupied with the problem of the tree, with the pattern of the disturbance, with the questions that spiraled outward from the simple observation that something in the Pollino landscape had changed.

He did not notice, on his way down, that he was being watched.

Farovald stood in the concealment of a rock outcropping perhaps three hundred paces away, his body held perfectly still, his breathing shallow and controlled. He had been watching the boy for the better part of an hour, had seen him discover the location where Italus had rooted herself in the new place, had watched him examine the tree and the burnt ground and the scattered evidence of movement. Farovald's hands were hidden in the folds of his rough cloth robe, palms downward, concealing the marks that had never quite faded, even after two hundred years. The old scars still bothered him sometimes, in damp weather or when he had been using his hands heavily. They ached now, a phantom pain that came from the memory of that afternoon in 589, from the moment when the sky had opened and the lightning had found him where he stood, his hand on the bark of the tree, his entire being connected in a moment of absolute terror and absolute knowledge to something that should not have been possible.

The boy was clever. He was careful. He was methodical in the way he examined the evidence. And now, Farovald knew, he would keep coming back. Boys like this, who thought in terms of systems and patterns and logic, would not be able to leave a mystery alone. He would construct excuses. He would invent reasons to return to the heights. He would come back again and again, trying to understand what had happened, trying to find some explanation that made sense within the framework of what he already knew to be true about how the world worked.

And eventually, the family would notice. The village would begin to talk. A fourteen-year-old boy could not simply disappear into the mountains day after day without someone beginning to ask questions. And if those questions became too persistent, if the interest of the adults became too direct, there might be people who would come up to the heights to investigate. People who might see the tree in its new location. People who might recognize that something was wrong. People who might decide that the wrong thing required action.

Farovald waited until Luca was nearly out of sight, moving down toward the main pastures, before he stepped out of his concealment and moved in the opposite direction, away from the village, into the higher fastnesses of the Pollino where few people ventured. He would need to think about what to do. He would need to decide whether the boy posed a threat to Italus, whether the boy's continued presence on the heights would eventually compromise the tree's safety, whether Farovald himself needed to intervene in the boy's patterns of discovery.

It was, after all, his responsibility to protect her. It had been his responsibility for two hundred years, ever since that moment in 589 when they had been bound together by lightning and burn and the knowledge of something vast passing through them both. And he had become very good at protecting her in ways that did not draw attention, in ways that kept her hidden from the ordinary sight of ordinary people.

But a clever boy with a good memory was not an ordinary obstacle.

Over the next three weeks, Luca returned to the heights six times. He came up with increasingly weak excuses. He told his father that the shepherd in the next valley had mentioned good grazing near the upper rocks. He told his mother that he had seen a wolf and was trying to track it to determine if it posed a danger to the flock. He told his younger sister that he was searching for medicinal herbs that his mother might be able to use for the village women who came to her with complaints of pain in their joints.

His father began to watch him with an expression that suggested deep thought and possible disapproval. His mother asked more questions about the herbs he was supposed to be searching for, questions that made it clear she knew he was not being entirely truthful. His sister, who was eleven and sharper than most, simply smiled when he told her about the herbs and made a point of not contradicting him directly, which was worse than if she had called him a liar.

The village, or at least the parts of the village that included the shepherds and the families who depended on them, began to whisper about the boy who kept disappearing into the mountains. There were jokes made in his presence about his dedication to the herd. There were comments made behind his back about whether he was spending his time properly, whether something up there on the heights had caught his attention in a way that was not entirely about sheep or herbs or wolves.

On his sixth trip, Luca was careful to bring the main flock higher than usual, justifying the movement to his uncle by pointing out that the lower pastures had been grazed pretty thoroughly and the animals needed fresh grass. His uncle, who was ordinarily willing to let Luca handle the herd with minimal supervision, agreed, though he gave Luca a look that suggested he was being humored rather than convinced.

Luca made his way to the place where the pine now stood, half-expecting it to have disappeared again, half-expecting to find some new mystery layered on top of the old one. But the tree was where it had been on his last visit. The earth around it had begun to settle. New grass was starting to grow in the disturbed areas. The roots that had been exposed were beginning to be covered by soil that had blown or washed back into place. In a few more weeks, if the weather cooperated, an observer who did not know to look for it would hardly notice that anything had changed.

Luca placed his hand on the scarred bark again, feeling for some kind of answer in the texture of the wood. The tree was warm in the afternoon sun. The scars were real. The displacement was real. But the explanation remained hidden, wrapped up in some system of causality that Luca did not have access to, that did not fit into the patterns he knew how to read.

He was so focused on the tree, on trying to understand through touch what his eyes could not quite see, that he did not notice the man until the man spoke.

"You've been coming here often."

Luca spun around, his hand dropping from the tree, his heart shifting into a faster rhythm. The man who stood perhaps twenty paces away was tall and lean, dressed in a simple robe of rough grey cloth. His hair was long and streaked with white, falling past his shoulders. His face was weathered, marked by lines that suggested either age or hardship or some combination of both. But his eyes were what stopped Luca from immediately running. They were clear, focused, and they held no obvious malice.

"I'm searching for herbs," Luca said quickly. "My mother uses them for remedies. I come up here because the best ones grow in the high places."

The man nodded slowly. He did not seem to be reacting with disbelief. That should have reassured Luca, but instead it made him more nervous. A man who believed an obvious lie was a man who was not particularly interested in the truth, and that could be dangerous in its own way.

"You've been coming here often," the man repeated, taking a step closer. "Not once. Not twice. Six times, at least, since the disturbance in the earth. I have been watching from the heights, and I have seen you searching. I have seen you at the tree, placing your hand on the bark, trying to understand something that you cannot yet articulate."

Luca's mind raced through possibilities. The man could be a village elder, come to confront him about his time on the heights. But the man wore no village clothes. He was not anyone Luca recognized, and in a village as small as the one he lived in, a stranger would have been noted and discussed. The man could be a hermit of some kind, a holy man living in the mountains the way the old stories talked about. That might explain both the appearance and the detailed knowledge of Luca's comings and goings.

"My name is Farovald," the man said. "I have made my home on these heights for a long time. I am a monk, of sorts. I spend much of my time in prayer and in observation of the natural world. I come to know the patterns of these mountains quite well."

Luca felt some of the tension in his shoulders ease slightly. A monk. That was acceptable. That was an explanation that fit the appearance, that made sense of the isolated life. And a monk would have reasons for being on the heights, for watching the land, for knowing the patterns of weather and animal life and, presumably, human intrusion.

"I am Luca," he said, in the formal way that one introduced oneself to a stranger who had introduced themselves. "I am a shepherd. My family tends flocks in the valleys below."

"I know," Farovald said. "I have heard you speak to the animals. I have listened to your footfalls on the stone. I know that you are a careful person, one who observes before acting, one who thinks through the implications of things before you move."

Luca was not sure whether this was meant as a compliment or a warning. He kept his expression neutral.

"But," Farovald continued, taking another step closer, "your excuses are growing thin. Your family has begun to notice. Your mother, particularly, is becoming concerned. Your father is approaching the point at which he will come up the mountain himself to understand what keeps drawing you here. And if he comes, others may follow. If others come, they will see what you have seen. They will ask questions. And those questions may lead to consequences that neither of us would prefer."

"What do you want?" Luca asked. His voice sounded younger than he would have liked. He steadied it. "Why are you telling me this?"

Farovald was silent for a long moment. He looked past Luca, toward the scarred pine, toward the tree that had moved and left evidence of its moving. When he spoke again, his voice was quieter than it had been before.

"I am suggesting," he said, "that you require a better excuse than herbs and wolves. The people of your village will accept a pattern of behavior if that behavior has a justification that they understand. They will accept repetition if that repetition serves a purpose they can comprehend."

"What kind of excuse?" Luca asked.

"Prayer," Farovald said. "The people of your village understand prayer. It is an acceptable reason for a young person to spend extended time alone in the high places. It suggests virtue rather than oddness. It suggests discipline rather than compulsion. If you were to come up to the heights regularly, and if you were to say that you were doing so in order to pray, in order to seek spiritual instruction in the silence of the mountains, your family would find that acceptable. Some would even find it admirable."

Luca considered this. It was true. Prayer was one of the acceptable reasons for any number of otherwise inexplicable behaviors. If he told his family that he was following a calling toward spiritual life, that he was spending time in the mountains seeking guidance, that he was attempting to develop a practice of meditation and prayer, his mother would likely approve. His father might not be pleased, but he would not forbid it. The village would nod approvingly and make jokes about the boy who was meant for a monastery rather than a shepherd's life, but there would be no real suspicion.

"You could come here," Farovald said, "ostensibly to pray with me. I do pray, after all, though perhaps not in the conventional manner. But you would have a justification for your presence. You would have a reason to bring you back again and again. You would have a framework within which to operate."

"And in exchange?" Luca asked. He was fourteen, and despite his careful nature, he understood that people did not offer help without expecting something in return.

Farovald smiled slightly. It was not a warm expression, but it was not entirely cold either. "In exchange," he said, "you do not speak to anyone about the tree. You do not mention it to your family, your friends, or the village elders. You observe if you wish. You think about it if you must. But you keep silent about what you have seen and what you have understood."

Luca looked from Farovald to the tree and back again. The scarred bark, the displaced earth, the roots that were slowly being reclaimed by soil and grass. The mystery of it. The wrongness of it. The knowledge that something had happened here that did not fit into the ordinary operation of the world. He thought about keeping that knowledge entirely to himself, about carrying it alone through the days and weeks that followed, about developing the habit of secrecy even as he developed the habit of returning to this place.

It seemed like a fair exchange. Or at least, it seemed like the only exchange available.

"All right," he said. "I will tell my family that I am coming to pray."

"Good," Farovald said. He turned slightly, gesturing toward the path that led deeper into the high Pollino, toward the places where few people ventured. "Come. I will show you the small cave where I spend most of my time during the daylight hours. You can bring a blanket or a mat if you wish, though it is not necessary. We can establish a pattern. You come to the heights, you spend some time in the cave, you spend some time in contemplation of the landscape, and then you return to the village. Your family will approve. The village will nod knowingly. And the secret will remain where it belongs, in the silence of the high places."

Luca hesitated for just a moment, feeling the weight of the commitment he was about to make. And then he stepped away from the tree and followed Farovald deeper into the mountains, his mind already beginning to construct the first careful habits of guardianship, the first intentional patterns of secrecy and protection that would, without knowing it, without having it named or acknowledged, bind him to the tree and to the monk and to the mystery of what had happened in the year 589, two hundred years before his birth, when lightning had struck and changed everything.

Behind them, as they moved away, the scarred pine stood quiet in the afternoon light, its roots settling deeper into the earth that had tried to hold it, its branches reaching upward toward a sky that had, once, tried to unmake it but had failed.
